messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slows a half-step behind the others and lets his eyes do the walking: the empty traces on the cart, the tools by the lower cut, the sheds, the roofline of the house, any window with a shutter half-open. He's looking for what's wrong. Fresh tracks in the dust, drag marks, where the mule went, anyone up on the terraces who shouldn't be. And he watches how the man in the apron holds himself. Is he glancing back into the house? Is that patience, or fear?

Low, to Bram and Sefa, without moving his lips much: "Quarry with no noise, and a warden who won't wave. Either the crew's on holiday or someone's sitting behind that door. Let's not all walk up in a bunch."

Then louder, friendly enough, a hand lifted and empty so the man can see it: "Morning! Maela Thorn sent us from Beregost, for the case. You'd be the warden?" He keeps a few strides of open ground between himself and the doorway and doesn't step closer until he's heard the answer.

? If it needs a roll, Pell's checking the yard with Perception +4 and reading the warden with Insight +4.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I sheathe my sword and walk into the yard, shield resting at my side. As I approach, I look over the sheds and quarry ledges for anyone else about.

“Morning. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I stop a few paces short of the doorway. “Quiet for a working day. Something happened?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
The silence sits wrong, like a held breath. Sefa keeps her hands open and well away from the book at her belt — no need to walk into a man's yard looking like trouble, especially not one with a ring of keys and arms folded like that. She glances once at the empty cart, the dropped tools, then starts forward a step or two ahead of the others, unhurried, letting the dust settle around their boots.

"Morning," she calls, warm but not loud. "We're the ones from Beregost — Maela Thorn sent us for her case." She stops short of the house, leaving a respectful distance between herself and the man. "You're the warden here?"

She studies him as she speaks: his face, his hands, whether he's been the only one moving in this yard.

scenes.narration:
The yard tells most of its story before anyone reaches the door. The dust holds yesterday's tracks: a crowd of hobnailed boots heading down the cart track towards Beregost, side by side and in no hurry. The prints spread out where men walked abreast, and in one place a dozen of them stand in a loose ring where somebody stopped to talk. Through the middle runs one line of hoof-prints beside a man's boots, a mule being led rather than driven. There are no drag marks, no scuffs where someone dug in his heels, and nothing has been knocked over. Up close, the tools by the lower cut have not been dropped in a panic. The wedges sit in a neat row on a ledge. One sledgehammer stands upright on its head with the haft pointing at the sky, the way a man leaves a thing he wants people to notice.

There is nobody on the terraces and nobody at the lifting frame. Every shed door is shut and every shutter closed, except the house's single front window, which stands open for the smoke and shows a table, a kettle and nothing else. Bram looks along the ledges and finds them empty. Sefa sees the same in the yard: one set of fresh tracks goes in and out of the house door and around to the woodpile behind it, and they all belong to the man in the apron.

He doesn't glance back into the house once. He watches their hands, Pell's empty one first, then Bram's on the sword hilt, then Sefa's well clear of her belt. His stance isn't fear. It's the heavy, set-jawed stillness of a man who has been angry for a long time and is tired of it.

He waits until all three of them have asked him the same thing.

"Warden. Osric Hale." He takes a breath through his nose. "Three of you asking. Yes."

To Bram's question he gives a short look across the empty yard, as though the answer were out there for anyone to see. "Crew walked. Noon bell, yesterday. Left the tools where they stood." He jerks his chin at the upright sledgehammer. "Tools are the house's. So they left them for the house."

He hasn't unfolded his arms. "The case. Thorn's case. It's inside, and it's sealed. I sealed it myself." He pauses. "Thorn paid for it. Paid somebody. Not me. Not a copper to this yard in three weeks, and eleven men's wages owing." He looks at each of them in turn, without heat, the way a man weighs stone. "Vandarren owns this pit. Vandarren's man in the Gate takes the money. So the case stays on my table till somebody tells me where her money went, and when my lads see theirs."

Then he steps back out of the doorway into the dim room and leaves the door open behind him. Inside, a small iron-bound box sits on the table beside the kettle, its lid crossed with cord and a blob of grey wax. Osric drops onto the bench next to it, sets one broad, dust-white hand flat on the lid, and stays there.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take my hand off the sword hilt and stay outside the threshold.

“Eleven men owed three weeks’ wages. I’d be angry too. But we’re hired carriers, Hale, not Vandarren’s collectors. If we go back empty-handed, the man in the Gate loses nothing. Your lads still go unpaid, and now so do we.”

I nod towards the box. “What’s owed altogether? And have you any word from his agent—a letter, a receipt, a name? Something we can put before Thorn while there’s still time to act.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops just short of the doorstep, hands still open at her sides, and lets a little of the road's tension ease out of her shoulders. She doesn't cross the threshold — that's his house, and he hasn't invited her in.

"Warden Hale," she says, "I won't stand here and tell you you've no right to be angry, because you have. Eleven men walked off and left their tools for the house — that's not a mob of rioters, that's men who trust their warden and are waiting for him to set it right." She nods toward the upright sledgehammer. "That's a thing left so it can't be missed. They're expecting you to come through for them."

She meets his eyes, calm. "We're not here to break your door down or walk out with what's yours. But Maela Thorn's not your enemy either — she's a woman in Beregost who paid for those dye-salts in good faith, and from your own account her coin went into somebody's pocket in Baldur's Gate long before it ever reached this yard. Vandarren's man. Not her."

She lets that sit for a heartbeat, then shifts her weight and offers the one thing she has: her word.

"Let us carry the case back to her before sunset — it's needed by then, or her buyer leaves without it — and I'll put your grievance in front of her myself, as clear as you've put it to us. Or if you'd rather, tell us who in the Gate takes Vandarren's money, and what proof you'd need to see, and we'll do what can be done about it. But the case won't help anyone sitting on your table while the light runs out."

She pauses, then asks plainly, with no edge: "What would it take, right now, for you to let that box go back to Beregost with us?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the others have the doorway and goes to lean on the frame of the open window instead, arms resting on the sill: close enough to talk, not close enough to crowd the man. He glances at the hand flat on the lid and leaves it alone.

"Eleven men, three weeks." He whistles low through his teeth. "My da broke stone on the harbour wall. Fist paid him late twice, and the second time he took his hammer home and kept it till they did." A small shrug. "So I won't tell you you're wrong."

He thinks for a breath, eyes on the sun's angle through the window.

"Here's my trouble, though. Thorn's coach leaves at sunset, and that case sitting on your table doesn't get your lads one copper. It just sits. And Vandarren's man in the Gate won't feel a thing till somebody squeezes him." He nods down the cart track. "Your crew went that way, didn't they? Beregost. Sitting in some taproom waiting on the same answer you are."

"So come with us. Carry it yourself, if you like. Your hand on it the whole road, seal and all. You put it in Thorn's hands and ask her to her face who she paid and when. If she paid Vandarren's man, she's got a receipt, and a buyer who'll want to know why the goods came late. That's a merchant with a grudge on your side instead of sitting in your way. If she didn't pay..." He spreads his fingers. "Then you've still got the case, and three witnesses who heard her say so."

He keeps his voice easy, but he's watching Osric's face the whole time, gauging whether there's more to this than wages. Is the man hiding something about Vandarren, or about the case itself?

"Who's Vandarren's man, by the way? Got a name? I know some doors in the Gate."

? Insight +4 on Osric if it's needed: is he honest about the wages and the case, and is there anything he's not saying?

scenes.narration:
Osric hears all three of them out without moving. Bram stays outside the threshold, Sefa stops at the step, and Pell leans in at the window, close enough to talk without crowding him. The warden's hand stays flat on the lid. Only his eyes move, from the man at the door to the woman at the step to the one at the window, and they rest longest on Pell while Pell talks about his father's hammer.

Pell watches him back, the way he would watch a doorman decide whether to let him in.

Pell can read the anger, and it's real: the jaw sets when he says "three weeks" and the weight of it shows in his shoulders. That much is honest. Past it, Osric's face gives Pell nothing more, just dust in the creases and a man thinking slowly. Pell can't find anything behind the wages to take hold of, and he can't say for certain that nothing is there.

Osric breathes in through his nose. He answers Bram first, because Bram asked for numbers.

"Sixty-one gold. Four silver. Eleven men, eighteen working days, cutters at cutters' rate." He nods sideways at a shelf behind him, where a fat ledger bound in grey canvas sits between a lamp and a crock of nails. "Tally-book has it to the copper." Then, to the rest of what Bram asked: "Name's Aubrin Teague. Vandarren's steward in the Gate. Counting-room off Windspell Street." He reaches under the lid of the bench without looking and pulls out a folded letter, softened by handling, and flattens it on the table next to the box. "His last. Five weeks back. *Wages to follow with the next cart.*" A short pause. "Cart came. Took salt. Brought nothing."

His eyes move to Sefa. He listens to the whole of what she says without interrupting, and when she finishes he doesn't soften, but he doesn't harden either.

"Didn't say Thorn's my enemy." He considers her. "Said she paid somebody. You say Vandarren's man. Maybe. Haven't seen it." He taps the letter once. "Your word's a good word, likely. Still yours. Not hers. Not Teague's."

Then he turns to the window, where Pell is, and keeps his eyes there for a long moment.

"My own hand on it." He seems to test the idea for weight. "Ask her to her face." Something in the set of his mouth eases a little, not into a smile. "That I'd do."

He gets up off the bench, heavily, and stands with his hand still on the case, looking out through the window past Pell at the yard: the cart, the frame, the row of sheds with their shut doors, the dark mouth of the lower cut beyond them.

"Can't walk off and leave her standing open, though." The way he says *her* makes it plain he means the quarry. "Thirty years. Sheds locked. Frame pinned, ropes in. Mule-shed's empty, no matter. Sluice-gate in the low cut wants shutting, or the seep backs up the drain by morning." He pauses, and his eyes stay on the lower cut a little longer than on the rest. "Hour's work. Less, with hands."

He picks up Teague's letter, folds it once, and puts it inside his apron. Then he lifts the iron-bound box off the table, tucks it under one arm as easily as a loaf, and takes the ring of keys from his belt. He comes out past Bram into the sun, pulls the house door shut, and locks it from outside with the case still under his arm. Then he sets off across the yard towards the first shed. The dust puffs white around his boots, and the lower cut waits at the far end of the yard. Its walls are stained darker than the rest of the quarry, and cool air drifts up out of it, smelling of standing water.

I nod towards the box. “What’s owed altogether? And have you any word from his agent—a letter, a receipt, a name? Something we can put before Thorn while there’s still time to act.”

Sefa Marrin: Sefa stops just short of the doorstep, hands still open at her sides, and lets a little of the road's tension ease out of her shoulders. She doesn't cross the threshold — that's his house, and he hasn't invited her in.

"Warden Hale," she says, "I won't stand here and tell you you've no right to be angry, because you have. Eleven men walked off and left their tools for the house — that's not a mob of rioters, that's men who trust their warden and are waiting for him to set it right." She nods toward the upright sledgehammer. "That's a thing left so it can't be missed. They're expecting you to come through for them."

She meets his eyes, calm. "We're not here to break your door down or walk out with what's yours. But Maela Thorn's not your enemy either — she's a woman in Beregost who paid for those dye-salts in good faith, and from your own account her coin went into somebody's pocket in Baldur's Gate long before it ever reached this yard. Vandarren's man. Not her."

She lets that sit for a heartbeat, then shifts her weight and offers the one thing she has: her word.

"Let us carry the case back to her before sunset — it's needed by then, or her buyer leaves without it — and I'll put your grievance in front of her myself, as clear as you've put it to us. Or if you'd rather, tell us who in the Gate takes Vandarren's money, and what proof you'd need to see, and we'll do what can be done about it. But the case won't help anyone sitting on your table while the light runs out."

She pauses, then asks plainly, with no edge: "What would it take, right now, for you to let that box go back to Beregost with us?"

"Eleven men, three weeks." He whistles low through his teeth. "My da broke stone on the harbour wall. Fist paid him late twice, and the second time he took his hammer home and kept it till they did." A small shrug. "So I won't tell you you're wrong."

He thinks for a breath, eyes on the sun's angle through the window.

"Here's my trouble, though. Thorn's coach leaves at sunset, and that case sitting on your table doesn't get your lads one copper. It just sits. messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa nods once — not eagerly, but like a woman who's decided. "Then we make the quarry fast, and you walk to Beregost with your hand on your own case, and put your question to Maela Thorn yourself. That's fairer than anything I could carry for you."

She walks after him, keeping a respectful few paces to his left, and lets her eyes follow his to the lower cut. The cool air and the smell of standing water reach her, and she doesn't like the way the warden's eyes linger there — not fear, exactly, but something he isn't saying.

"I'm no labourer," she admits, "but two hands are two hands, and I can carry, haul on a rope, or hold a light where the sun won't reach. Tell me what needs doing and I'll do my part. The sooner that sluice is shut, the sooner we're all on the road."

She glances toward the dark mouth of the cut, then back at him. "Is there anything down there besides the seep? You'd know the signs better than we would." Her tone is quiet, not prying — a hospice worker's habit of asking after what hurts.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell pushes off the sill and falls in beside Osric. He walks at the man's shoulder rather than behind him, glancing once at the box under his arm and then letting it be.

"Hour's work, less with hands. Let's make it less." He raises his voice just enough to carry back to the others. "Bram, you know a lifting frame from caravan yards? Pinning it and coiling the ropes is muscle work. Sefa, you could take the tally-book and the letter from him and count it against what he told us, so we've got it straight for Thorn." He glances at Osric. "If you'll let her. Your book, your call."

To Osric, quieter: "Sheds I can do fast. Give me the keys and point. Locks and I get on." He doesn't reach for the ring, just holds out a hand and waits.

Then he jerks his chin at the dark mouth of the lower cut, at its stained walls and the cool air coming up out of it.

"And I'll come down with you to that sluice. Never shut one. Want to see how it's done." His tone is easy and curious, but his eyes stay on the cut and the ground leading into it. He's looking for fresh tracks that aren't Osric's or the crew's, for water where water shouldn't be, for anything down there worth a long look from a man who's worked this pit thirty years. "Is it stiff, that gate? Or is something else wrong down there?"

He keeps a loose hand near his shortsword's hilt without touching it, and he walks on the side of Osric nearest the cut.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’ll lend a hand. Better an hour here than an argument till sunset.”

I fall into step beside Osric. “That lower cut—anything we should know before going down? Bad footing, loose stone, deep water?”

I glance towards the lifting frame. “Put me on the heavy work. Show me what needs pinning and which ropes need bringing in.” I help secure it as he directs, keeping clear of suspended gear.

scenes.narration:
Osric hears Sefa out without breaking stride. When she offers to hold a light where the sun won't reach, he gives her a short sideways look, the first that seems to take her for something other than trouble.

"Fair." He walks a few more steps. Then, about the cut: "Water. Cold. Air sits heavy low down, so nobody lingers. You do the job and come up." Nothing in his voice changes. It sounds like a rule a man says so often he no longer hears it.

Bram's question gets a longer answer, and Osric slows down to give it. He stops at the edge of the yard and points with the hand that isn't holding the box. "Footing's good on the crew's track. Planked where it's wet." Then he moves his hand across the eastern half of the yard: the sheds, the spoil heaps, the ground sloping down towards the lower cut. "Whole hill's old workings underneath. Three hundred years of men digging. Some are shored. Some were forgotten. Keep to where the dust is trodden." He looks at each of them in turn to be sure they heard. "Loose stone on the top terrace. Nobody's going up there today."

Pell holds out his hand, and Osric looks at it longer than he looked at Pell's face. Then he works three square-headed iron keys off the ring, leaves the rest at his belt, and drops the three into Pell's palm. "Square heads. Sheds. Back in my hand before we walk." The tally-book, he says, stays where it is. "House is locked. Book comes with me to Beregost." He looks at Sefa. "She can read it on the road. Every line." He doesn't take the letter out of his apron.

Pell offers to come down to the sluice, and Osric just nods. "Suit yourself. Gate's stiff. Rust. Wants two hands on the wheel." He doesn't answer the second question, whether something else is wrong down there, and he isn't looking at the cut when he leaves it unanswered.

---

The work goes the way honest work goes: dusty, simple, and faster with more hands.

The lifting frame is a pair of tall timber shear-legs over a windlass drum, built more heavily than anything Bram has seen in a caravan yard, but the idea is the same. Osric shows him once, and he doesn't need to see it twice. Bram leans his weight into the crank to take the slack off the drum, holding it while Osric drops the iron locking-pin through the pawl, then walks the boom down until it rests on its trestle. He stays clear of the hook as it swings and lets it come to rest against the leg. The ropes come in after that, three long hawsers stiff with chalk. Bram coils them on his forearm the way he would on a wagon bed, and Osric watches him do it and says nothing, which from Osric is close to approval. Sefa takes the end of each rope as it comes off the frame and walks it out straight so it doesn't kink, then carries the coils to the rope-shed two at a time. It's heavier work than she'd like, and her arms tell her so.

Pell goes down the row of sheds with the square keys. They aren't difficult locks. These are country padlocks, honest iron, made to keep goats and boys out. Inside the tool-shed are racks of wedges and feathers and spare hafts. The rope-shed fills as Sefa brings the coils. The mule-shed is empty, with a manger of hay and the smell of an animal that left yesterday. Pell snaps each lock shut and tries it once with a tug.

The last shed is different. It stands lower than the others, at the head of the slope where the yard falls away into the lower cut, and it's built half into the hillside. Its door swells against the frame from the damp. Inside is a cutting-shed for wet weather: a long bench of half-dressed white blocks, chisels laid in a row, a water-butt. In the middle of the floor stands an iron brazier, cold. A crust of ash sits in its bowl, and the ash is pale pink, the colour of a rose petal left in the sun. A faint smell clings to the room, under the damp and the chalk. It's sweet and dry, a little like burnt sugar and a little like flour. The floor here is planked rather than packed earth, the boards grey with age and stained dark along the wall nearest the cut.

Behind Pell, Osric has come down the slope with the box under his arm and stopped at the plank walk leading into the lower cut. Bram drops the last coil in the rope-shed, and Sefa comes back across the yard dusting her hands on her skirts. Below them the lower cut opens downward in stained steps, its walls darker than the rest of the quarry, until a sheet of still black water fills the bottom. At the water's edge stands a wooden sluice-frame with an iron wheel, its spokes red with rust. The cool air keeps rising out of it, steady as breath.

Pell stepped up beside Osric, suggested Sefa check the tally-book and letter against what Osric told you, asked for the keys, and offered to come down to the sluice, asking whether the gate was stiff or something else was wrong.

Osric gave Sefa a short sideways look when she offered a light, the first that seemed to take her for something other than trouble. "Fair." About the cut he said: "Water. Cold. Air sits heavy low down, so nobody lingers. You do the job and come up." It sounded like a rule he says so often he no longer hears it.

To you he gave a longer answer, slowing to give it. He stopped at the edge of the yard and pointed out the sheds, the spoil heaps and the ground sloping to the lower cut. Footing is good on the crew's track, planked where wet. "Whole hill's old workings underneath. Three hundred years of men digging. Some are shored. Some were forgotten. Keep to where the dust is trodden." He looked at each of you in turn. The top terrace has loose stone and nobody is going up there today.

Pell held out a hand, and Osric looked at it longer than at Pell's face, then worked three square-headed iron keys off his ring and dropped them in Pell's palm. They are for the sheds and must come back to his hand before you walk. The tally-book stays with him, since the house is locked and it goes to Beregost. Sefa can read it on the road, every line. He didn't take the letter out of his apron. To Pell's offer to see the sluice he nodded: "Gate's stiff. Rust. Wants two hands on the wheel." He didn't answer whether anything else was wrong down there, and he wasn't looking at the cut as he left it unanswered.

The work goes dusty, simple and faster with more hands. The lifting frame is a pair of tall timber shear-legs over a windlass drum, built more heavily than anything you've seen in a caravan yard, but the idea is the same. Osric shows you once, and you don't need it twice. You lean into the crank to take the slack off the drum and hold it while Osric drops the iron locking-pin through the pawl, then walk the boom down until it rests on its trestle. You stay clear of the hook and let it come to rest against the leg. Three long hawsers stiff with chalk come in next. You coil them on your forearm as you would on a wagon bed, and Osric watches and says nothing, which from him is close to approval. Sefa takes the end of each rope as it comes off, walks it out straight so it doesn't kink, and carries the coils to the rope-shed two at a time. Pell goes down the row of sheds with the keys, snapping each lock shut and tugging it.

The last shed stands lower than the others, at the head of the slope where the yard falls into the lower cut, built half into the hillside. Pell is at it as you drop the last coil in the rope-shed. Sefa comes back across the yard dusting her hands on her skirts. Osric has come down the slope with the box under his arm and stopped at the plank walk into the lower cut. Below, the cut opens downward in stained steps, its walls darker than the rest of the quarry, until a sheet of still black water fills the bottom. At the water's edge stands a wooden sluice-frame with an iron wheel, its spokes red with rust. The cool air keeps rising out of it, steady as breath.

She glances toward the dark mouth of the cut, then back at him. "Is there anything down there besides the seep? You'd know the signs better than we would." Her tone is quiet, not prying — a hospice worker's habit of asking after what hurts.

I fall into step beside Osric. “That lower cut—anything we should know before going down? Bad footing, loose stone, deep water?”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops in the doorway of the low shed instead of snapping the lock straight away. He breathes shallow through his nose and pulls the collar of his jerkin up over his mouth out of habit. Lower City cellars taught him not to gulp air that smells sweet.

He doesn't touch the brazier at first. He crouches beside it and looks: how deep the ash lies, whether there's anything unburnt in it, any scrap of wrapping, wax or cord like the box's seal. He wets a fingertip, takes the smallest pinch of the pink crust, rubs it, sniffs it at arm's length, and folds it into a twist of rag from his pouch. Then he moves to the dark-stained boards along the cut-side wall. Is the stain water seeping up from below, or something spilled or dragged? Are any boards newer, loose, or nailed differently from the rest? He runs a knife-tip along the seams to check whether one lifts, and he glances at the water-butt and the chisels to see whether someone was working here yesterday or not for weeks.

Without turning, pitched to carry to Sefa and no further: "Sefa. Come smell this, but don't breathe deep. Pink ash and burnt sugar. That's no stonecutter's fire."

Then he steps back out, pulls the swollen door to without locking it yet, and walks the few steps down to where Osric waits at the plank walk. He holds up the folded rag between two fingers, easy, not accusing.

"Your wet-weather shed. Somebody's been burning something in that brazier that isn't coal. Pink ash, sweet smell." He watches the man's face. "That the dye-salts? Thorn's goods? Or did somebody else have a fire down here?" A beat, glancing at the black water. "And is that why the air down there sits heavy?"

He keeps the third key in his hand rather than handing it back.

? Investigation +4 on the shed: what was burned, and what's under the stained boards. Insight +4 on Osric's answer, if it's needed.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I stop at the head of the plank walk and look over the route to the wheel, checking the planks and supports.

“Osric. You didn’t answer Pell’s other question. Anything wrong down there besides rust and bad air? We need to know before we put hands on it.”

I take out my rope. “Let’s have a line on whoever works the wheel, with someone holding it up here. If a man gets dizzy, we haul him out—not send another down after him.”

I look to Sefa. “If we need light, can yours do without a flame?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stays at the top of the plank walk, not crowding the descent. She picks up a flat white stone from the yard, turns it over in her palm, and speaks a low word. The Lantern's light blooms on it, clean and steady, with no flame to gutter.

She holds it out to Pell. "Carry that down, or set it on the rail while you work the wheel. It won't smoke or burn low like a lamp." Then she touches two fingers lightly to his wrist and murmurs a short prayer, asking the Lantern to steady his hands. "For the wheel," she says. "The light won't fail you, and neither will I. But I'll keep this side of the cut unless you call."

She lets them go down, then folds her arms and watches the plank walk and the black water below, listening for anything that isn't boots on planking.

She tells you it won't smoke or sink low the way a lamp does, and holds it out for you to carry down or to rest beside you while you work the wheel. Then she crosses her arms and watches the walk and the black water, listening.

scenes.narration:
Pell stops on the threshold of the low shed and leaves the lock alone. He pulls his collar up over his mouth and nose and breathes shallow, then crouches beside the cold brazier without touching it.

The ash is a thin crust over ordinary coal clinker, and nothing else is in the bowl: no scrap of wrapping, no wax, no cord. At the bottom, where the fire never quite reached, a few grains survived. They are rose-white, glassy and coarse, like rock salt that has been left out in the sun. The crust breaks crisp under his wet fingertip, so the fire burned out days ago, not weeks. He holds the pinch at arm's length and sniffs once, carefully. For a single breath his eyelids go heavy, the way they do at the end of a long night's work, though the morning is young and he isn't tired. He yawns behind his collar before he can stop it. Then the feeling is gone. He folds the pinch into a twist of rag and puts it away.

The bench tells him the rest. There's yesterday's chalk on the chisels, and fresh dust on the half-dressed blocks. Men worked in here until the strike, in a shed that turns sleepy when its fire burns sweet.

The stain along the cut-side wall isn't spillage, and nothing has been dragged across it. It's water coming up from below. The nails in those boards are the same old square heads as everywhere else, and nobody has touched them in years. But when he slides his knife-tip into a seam, it sinks a finger's depth into the grain as easily as into cheese. He taps the board with the pommel and gets a hollow sound back. A cold breath rises through the seam, smelling of the same standing water as the cut below. There's empty space under that floor, and the wood over it is rotten.

He steps back out, pulls the swollen door to without locking it, and walks down to the head of the plank walk.

Bram has been looking over the walk the way he'd look over a ford before he trusted a wagon to it, and the walk is sound. The planks are thick and newer than the sheds, spiked into cut stone steps that drop in tiers towards the black water. The crew kept their track in repair. Only the last stretch is bare. At the bottom a broad ledge of wet stone runs along the water to the sluice-frame, dark with seep, and from up here nobody could say what lies under it.

Sefa picks a flat white stone out of the dust and speaks a word over it. Light blooms on it, clean and steady, bright enough to throw shadows at noon. There's no flame in it to gutter or smoke. She holds it out to Pell, and then she lays two fingers on his wrist and murmurs a few words. Something warm and steady settles into his hands under her touch, and it's still there when she lets go.

Osric looks at the rag Pell holds up, then at Pell. He breathes in through his nose.

"Salt. Thorn's salt." He tips his head towards the cut. "Grows on the walls down there. Pink crust. Lads scrape it in the wet, I case it." He glances at the shed. "Chips get in with the coal. Fire burns sweet. Shed goes sleepy. Told 'em. No salt in the fire." He pauses. "Air's heavy. Always was."

Pell reads him as he would read a doorman. The part about the salt comes out easily. Osric has said it before, and it costs him nothing. The last part is different. It isn't a lie, but it's a door shut on something. While he says it, his eyes are on the water and not on Pell, and he says it like a man who has stood at that edge and thought about it more than once.

Then Bram asks him straight out, with the rope already in his hands, and the warden looks at the coil for a moment before he answers.

"Lost a man down there. Tobin Reed. Three years back." His voice stays level. "Four feet of water. Found him in it. Face down, like he'd gone to sleep." A short silence. "Drink, I wrote."

Pell catches the word *wrote*. Osric didn't say *was*. Whatever went into the book, he doesn't believe it himself.

"Line's good," Osric says to Bram, and he means it. "Wheel wants two hands on it. Me and one. Line on both. Down, wheel, up. Nobody sits."

He looks at the iron-bound box under his arm, then at the three of them. Then he bends and sets it on a flat block at the head of the walk, square in the sun, where anyone on the walk or at the wheel can see it. He leaves his hand on the lid a moment longer than he needs to. "Stays there."

He straightens up and holds out his hand for the end of Bram's rope. Below them the cool air keeps rising out of the cut, and on the ledge the rusted wheel waits by the still black water.

messages.text:
“Then we treat it as bad air, not drink. First sign of dizziness, we come straight back. If either of us drops, nobody follows—haul us out.”

I pass Osric a loop, then tie one around myself, leaving rope between us so we can both work the wheel. Before descending, I check that the fifty-foot line will reach the ledge with enough left for Pell and Sefa to haul from safe ground. If it won’t, I stay put.

“Pell, Sefa—can you tend the line? Keep it out of the water.”

If they’re ready and the rope reaches, I go down with Osric along the maintained track, testing the wet footing before approaching the wheel.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa watches the warden set the case in the sun, square and visible, and something in the careful way he leaves his hand on it tells her he means it as an oath.

When he holds out his hand for the rope, she shakes her head once, not enough to argue, just enough to offer herself.

"I won't pretend I can hold a rope against a falling man better than Bram," she says. "But I'll stand anchor-side and watch the line, and I can burn a word into the stone so it floats above the water if anyone drops it. Light won't go out under the water." She pauses, then adds, quieter: "If a man goes down, call me down and I'll bring him back if he can be brought."

She looks to Bram and Osric, then steps clear of the plank walk and takes up a post just behind Bram's right shoulder, one foot set against bare stone. The glow on the white stone pulses once, steady.

"Tie it fast," she says. "And send one down at a time. I'll watch the water."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lowers the rag slowly and looks from the pink crust on the cut walls to the black water. Then he looks at Osric, and his voice has none of its easiness left.

"I sniffed that ash at arm's length, one pinch, and nearly yawned my jaw off." He taps the twist of rag in his pouch. "Your shed goes sleepy when it burns. Down there it's a whole wall of the stuff, wet, with the air sitting on it. I don't think Tobin was drunk." He leaves it at that. It isn't his to rub in.

He shrugs off his pack and pulls out his own coil of silk rope. "So we do it your way. Down, wheel, up, nobody sits. And a bit more." He soaks a strip of rag from his waterskin and ties it over his nose and mouth, then holds out another wet strip to Osric. "Wet cloth on the face. It won't stop it, but it won't hurt. And we count. Sefa, count out loud from up top. If either of us stops answering, or slows on the wheel, Bram hauls, no arguing."

He ties the silk rope around his own chest, under the arms, with a knot he can slip, and hands the free end to Bram. "You're the anchor. You've got the arms for two of us. Sefa, keep the light on our faces, not the water. I want you to see our eyes."

To Osric, short: "I'll be your second pair of hands. I'm light, and if I go soft Bram can pull me up like a sack of washing. Better me than him in chain in four feet of water."

Before he starts down, quieter, just to the warden: "One more thing. Floor in that low shed, cut-side wall, is rotten through and hollow underneath. Cold air coming up the seams. Old working under it?" He watches the answer. "Nobody stands on those boards till you've seen to it."

Then he steps onto the plank walk behind Osric, testing each tread. He stays on the crew's track, keeps one hand on the rope, and keeps his eyes on the ledge by the sluice-frame, looking for anything that isn't stone and water.

? I'm keeping Sefa's Guidance for whatever check the wheel or the air throws at me down there.

scenes.narration:
Bram ties a loop for Osric, ties one around himself with a fathom of slack between them, and walks the free end down the plank walk to see where it runs out. The walk doesn't go straight down. It switches back across the stepped tiers, and from the head of the walk to the bare ledge it's a good forty-odd feet of planking. With two men tied a fathom apart at the bottom, the tail of a fifty-foot line ends on the second tier from the top. Nobody could haul from there without standing on the walk themselves. Bram has the measure of it before he reaches the bottom step, and by his own rule he stays at the top. Osric looks at the coil, then at the drop, and grunts. The loop around his own chest stays where it is, and the hempen line now runs from Bram at the head of the walk down to the warden.

Sefa takes her post behind Bram's right shoulder with one foot braced on bare stone. The lit stone in her hand throws its clean light down the first two tiers. Osric glances back at her once when she says *one at a time*. He doesn't argue.

Pell's words about the ash and Tobin land on the warden and stay there. Osric doesn't answer them. He breathes in through his nose, takes the wet strip of rag out of Pell's hand, and ties it over his beard without a word. Pell asks about the shed floor, and Osric looks back up the slope at the low shed for a moment.

"Old working. Shed's built over the mouth of it." A pause. "Knew the boards were soft. On my list." He turns to the walk. "Nobody stands there."

Pell ties his silk line under his arms with a slip-knot and presses the free end into Bram's hand, over the hempen one. Then he follows Osric down.

The walk is as sound as it looked. The planks are thick and dry under the chalk, and every tread Pell tests holds. Osric goes first and doesn't hurry. The air turns cooler at each tier, and then heavy, the way a cellar's air is heavy. Through the wet cloth Pell catches the faintest sweetness, like flour in a cold bakery. The walls close in on either side, and the pink crust shows on them now. It runs in ribbons along the seams and glitters wet where Sefa's light reaches.

At the bottom the planking stops and the ledge begins. Osric steps off onto it and walks the ten feet to the sluice-frame without looking down. He's walked that stone for thirty years. He sets both hands on the rusted wheel.

Pell comes after him, keeping his eyes on the ledge. It's dark with seep and slick with chalk mud, and the black water lies an arm's length to his right. He tests the first step and it holds. On the second step he feels the give an instant before he hears it. What has looked like stone is a skin of chalk and seep laid over old timber, and the timber crumbles under his heel like wet bread.

The ledge opens under him.

He drops eight feet through a rush of rotten wood and wet chalk. The slack of the silk line pays out across the planks above, and the rope snaps taut around Bram's fist at the moment Pell hits the bottom. He comes down hard on one hip and shoulder in cold water. It knocks the breath out of him and leaves him bruised and shaken, with nothing broken. Then the lip of the hole comes down after him. A squared block of white stone, dressed on its faces, tips off the broken edge, and its corner lands across his left shin under the water. It pins the leg to the floor of the working.

Above, the silk line hangs straight up through the hole with a man on the end of it, and nobody can lift him while the stone holds.

Down here the water comes up to Pell's chest. It's cold enough to make his teeth ache, and it's still, apart from a thin trickle of seep from a crack in the far wall. A tidemark of pink crust runs round the walls a hand's width above the surface. The working is a low chamber cut square, about the size of a small room, and the timber deck that rotted over it was laid across it a long time ago. The air is heavier here than it was at the ledge. The sweetness comes through the wet rag, faint and patient. Light falls in through the hole in a grey shaft, and in it Pell can see what holds him.

It's no fallen rubble. The block was cut to stand upright in the wall. It has fallen with its broad face tilted up out of the water, and on that face someone carved a sun a long time ago. It's a round disc with straight rays, and a ring of small, careful marks runs around it like a mason's tally. Where the block stood, the wall behind shows a patch of old grey plaster, smoother than the cut stone around it. One of the rotten deck-beams lies across the corner of the chamber, half sunk, black with wet but still whole.

The block's lower edge is rough-broken and jagged, and it has bitten into his leg. He can feel the weight pressing the torn flesh closed. A rogue who carries the potions knows what that means. The weight is the only thing holding the wound shut. When the stone comes off, the leg will open and bleed hard. Whoever moves it needs a healing ready the moment it shifts, a potion down his throat or Sefa's light on him, or he'll go under. One pinned man can't move a block that size alone. Two up top with a rope and that beam for a lever could do it in a few minutes.

On the ledge Osric has let go of the wheel. He's down on his knees on the stone he trusts, at the edge of the hole, with Bram's line tight across his back. He looks down at Pell in the water, then at the carved sun, and for a moment he doesn't breathe through his nose or anywhere else.

"Don't sit." His voice is rough. "Keep talking. Keep your head up." Then he shouts up the walk without turning: "Old working under the ledge! Bare stone's bad! Nobody comes on it but by the planks!"

The seep goes on trickling in through the crack in the far wall.

Sefa takes her post behind Bram's right shoulder with one foot braced on bare stone. The lit stone in her hand throws its clean light down the first two tiers. Osric glances back at her once when she says *one at a time*. He doesn't argue.

Pell's words about the ash and Tobin land on the warden and stay there. Osric doesn't answer them. He breathes in through his nose, takes the wet strip of rag out of Pell's hand, and ties it over his beard without a word. Pell asks about the shed floor, and Osric looks back up the slope at the low shed for a moment.

"Old working. Shed's built over the mouth of it." A pause. "Knew the boards were soft. On my list." He turns to the walk. "Nobody stands there."

Pell ties his silk line under his arms with a slip-knot and presses the free end into Bram's hand, over the hempen one. Then he follows Osric down.

The walk is as sound as it looked. The planks are thick and dry under the chalk, and every tread Pell tests holds. Osric goes first and doesn't hurry. The air turns cooler at each tier, and then heavy, the way a cellar's air is heavy. Through the wet cloth Pell catches the faintest sweetness, like flour in a cold bakery. The walls close in on either side, and the pink crust shows on them now. It runs in ribbons along the seams and glitters wet where Sefa's light reaches.

At the bottom the planking stops and the ledge begins. Osric steps off onto it and walks the ten feet to the sluice-frame without looking down. He's walked that stone for thirty years. He sets both hands on the rusted wheel.

Pell comes after him, keeping his eyes on the ledge. It's dark with seep and slick with chalk mud, and the black water lies an arm's length to his right. He tests the first step and it holds. On the second step he feels the give an instant before he hears it. What has looked like stone is a skin of chalk and seep laid over old timber, and the timber crumbles under his heel like wet bread.

The ledge opens under him.

He drops eight feet through a rush of rotten wood and wet chalk. The slack of the silk line pays out across the planks above, and the rope snaps taut around Bram's fist at the moment Pell hits the bottom. He comes down hard on one hip and shoulder in cold water. It knocks the breath out of him and leaves him bruised and shaken, with nothing broken. Then the lip of the hole comes down after him. A squared block of white stone, dressed on its faces, tips off the broken edge, and its corner lands across his left shin under the water. It pins the leg to the floor of the working.

Above, the silk line hangs straight up through the hole with a man on the end of it, and nobody can lift him while the stone holds.

Down here the water comes up to Pell's chest. It's cold enough to make his teeth ache, and it's still, apart from a thin trickle of seep from a crack in the far wall. A tidemark of pink crust runs round the walls a hand's width above the surface. The working is a low chamber cut square, about the size of a small room, and the timber deck that rotted over it was laid across it a long time ago. The air is heavier here than it was at the ledge. The sweetness comes through the wet rag, faint and patient. Light falls in through the hole in a grey shaft, and in it Pell can see what holds him.

It's no fallen rubble. The block was cut to stand upright in the wall. It has fallen with its broad face tilted up out of the water, and on that face someone carved a sun a long time ago. It's a round disc with straight rays, and a ring of small, careful marks runs around it like a mason's tally. Where the block stood, the wall behind shows a patch of old grey plaster, smoother than the cut stone around it. One of the rotten deck-beams lies across the corner of the chamber, half sunk, black with wet but still whole.

The block's lower edge is rough-broken and jagged, and it has bitten into his leg. He can feel the weight pressing the torn flesh closed. A rogue who carries the potions knows what that means. The weight is the only thing holding the wound shut. When the stone comes off, the leg will open and bleed hard. Whoever moves it needs a healing ready the moment it shifts, a potion down his throat or Sefa's light on him, or he'll go under. One pinned man can't move a block that size alone. Two up top with a rope and that beam for a lever could do it in a few minutes.

On the ledge Osric has let go of the wheel. He's down on his knees on the stone he trusts, at the edge of the hole, with Bram's line tight across his back. He looks down at Pell in the water, then at the carved sun, and for a moment he doesn't breathe through his nose or anywhere else.

"Don't sit." His voice is rough. "Keep talking. Keep your head up." Then he shouts up the walk without turning: "Old working under the ledge! Bare stone's bad! Nobody comes on it but by the planks!"

The seep goes on trickling in through the crack in the far wall.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't rush the ledge. She moves only along the planking, to where she can look straight down into the hole, and holds her light over it so it falls on Pell and Osric's faces, not on the black water below.

"Pell," she calls, voice steady, the way she'd speak across a sick ward. "Breathe. Tell me if the line's cutting you, and if your hands and feet will move. Don't fight the rope — Bram has you."

She plants her feet on the last sound plank, one hand on the rail, and lets the stone's light flood the shaft. "I'm no good at hauling, but I've light and I've healing. Say the word and I'll put warmth into you from here." She looks to Bram's straining arm, then to Osric. "Can the rope be shifted onto something solid — a rail-post, a spike — so we can pull him without tearing him against the edge? Or is there room to lower him gently to a proper floor under there?"

There is no panic in her, only that hospice calm, the kind that leaves room for other people's courage. "Keep talking, Pell. You're not going to die in the dark; I won't allow it."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I brace on solid ground, keeping both lines taut without trying to wrench Pell free.

“Sefa, help me hold these. Don’t go onto that ledge.”

I call down, loud and steady. “Pell! What’s pinning you, and is your head clear of the water? Can you free it if the line takes your weight?”

“Osric, back onto the planks if you can do it safely. No more weight by that hole.”

Once Sefa has a firm hold, I work the hempen line around a sound anchoring point if there’s one within reach, keeping tension throughout. I keep talking to Pell while we find out what must move before we haul.

scenes.narration:
Bram sets his heels on the bare cut stone at the head of the walk, takes the strain on both lines, and leaves them still. Pell's silk line hangs taut over the planking, but not tight enough to drag anyone against an edge. The hempen line runs down past the switchbacks to Osric. Bram has stopped pulling on either.

The walk has a rail on its outer side, a run of split poles lashed to posts. The first post sits a stride below Bram, set into a socket cut in the rock and wedged with iron. Bram leans on it with his shoulder before he trusts it, and it doesn't move. He takes two turns of the hempen line around it and a half-hitch over them, and keeps the tension on the whole time. Now the post holds the warden. Bram has his right hand free and the silk line in his left.

Sefa goes down the switchbacks one tread at a time, on planks only. On the last sound plank she stops with one hand on the rail. The broken lip of the hole is right in front of her, an arm's length past the end of the planking. She holds the stone out over the shaft, and its light falls straight down. The darkness turns into grey water, a jagged rim of rotten timber, and the tilted white face of the block. Her voice carries across the cut the way a voice carries across a ward at night.

Bram's shout booms off the walls after hers.

Osric doesn't move. He's on the far side of the hole, the sluice side, and the hole lies between him and the planks. He looks at it, then down at the stone under his knees, and puts the heel of his hand on it and presses.

"Sluice footing's rock. Frame's bolted in it." He doesn't raise his voice to Bram, but it reaches the top. "That gap's no place to step over. I stay this side. Low." He stretches out flat on his belly, with the rope across his back running up to the rail-post. Lying like that, his weight is as far from the edge as he can get it.

Sefa asks about lowering Pell to a proper floor, and Osric gives her a short look across the hole.

"He's on the floor."

Then he jerks his head at the water, at the black deck-beam lying half-sunk across the corner of the chamber.

"Beam goes under the block. Low edge, rough side. Rope round the far end, up to the lip. Two haul, the beam lifts, block tips off him." He breathes in through his nose. "Shifted blocks forty years. Comes up easy with the beam. Sits there a week without it."

Sefa's light shows her what Osric is describing. The block lies tilted with its carved face up: a sun disc with straight rays and a ring of small cut marks around it. It's the sunburst that Lathander's people cut over their doors and on their altar-cloths, cut here into a stone at the bottom of a quarry. The jagged lower edge has gone into the water, and the leg is under it. A hospice novice has seen this kind of wound on the docks, when a cargo net gave way. The stone has bitten in and is holding the torn flesh shut by its own weight. While the block stays put, the leg won't bleed much. Once it lifts, the wound will open and bleed hard, all at once. Whoever lifts it needs healing ready at that same moment: a potion down his throat, or her light on him.

The wall behind the block, where it once stood, shows a square patch of old grey plaster. Every surface in the working is wet: the cut stone, the pink tidemark, the rotten wood. The plaster is the only thing down there that looks dry.

The seep keeps trickling from the crack in the far wall, and the water has risen a hair's breadth against the tidemark.

 Sefa holds the stone low over the lip, angled so its light falls on the face below her and leaves the water dark. She talks down to him the whole time, unhurried and steady. When she asked about an anchor, Bram's half-hitch on the rail-post had already answered her: that post holds the warden's line now. Osric answered the rest flat: there's nowhere lower to put a man than the bottom. Her offer of warmth goes down the shaft with her voice and stays offered. The Lantern's light sits ready in her hands, unspent.

Up at the head of the walk, Bram keeps the silk line steady in his left hand. It's taut and he isn't hauling, so nothing pulls the pinned leg against the stone.

*(Out of game: none of these needed a roll, because nothing in them was uncertain. Calming him, lighting the shaft and holding the lines steady are plain actions, and the anchor and the "lower him to a floor" questions were answered by Bram's knot and Osric's reply. Sefa's healing is an offer until her player says she casts it. And Bram can't hold "Sefa's line" because she doesn't have one: Bram holds Pell's silk line himself and Osric's hempen line is tied to the post, so whether Sefa helps hold is her player's call next round.)*

Bram Halloway: I brace on solid ground, keeping both lines taut without trying to wrench Pell free.

“Sefa, help me hold these. Don’t go onto that ledge.”

I call down, loud and steady. “Pell! What’s pinning you, and is your head clear of the water? Can you free it if the line takes your weight?”

“Osric, back onto the planks if you can do it safely. No more weight by that hole.”

Once Sefa has a firm hold, I work the hempen line around a sound anchoring point if there’s one within reach, keeping tension throughout. I keep talking to Pell while we find out what must move before we haul.

Your narration:
<<<
Bram sets his heels on the bare cut stone at the head of the walk, takes the strain on both lines, and leaves them still. Pell's silk line hangs taut over the planking, but not tight enough to drag anyone against an edge. The hempen line runs down past the switchbacks to Osric. Bram has stopped pulling on either.

The walk has a rail on its outer side, a run of split poles lashed to posts. The first post sits a stride below Bram, set into a socket cut in the rock and wedged with iron. Bram leans on it with his shoulder before he trusts it, and it doesn't move. He takes two turns of the hempen line around it and a half-hitch over them, and keeps the tension on the whole time. Now the post holds the warden. Bram has his right hand free and the silk line in his left.

Sefa goes down the switchbacks one tread at a time, on planks only. On the last sound plank she stops with one hand on the rail. The broken lip of the hole is right in front of her, an arm's length past the end of the planking. She holds the stone out over the shaft, and its light falls straight down. The darkness turns into grey water, a jagged rim of rotten timber, and the tilted white face of the block. Her voice carries across the cut the way a voice carries across a ward at night.

Bram's shout booms off the walls after hers.

Osric doesn't move. He's on the far side of the hole, the sluice side, and the hole lies between him and the planks. He looks at it, then down at the stone under his knees, and puts the heel of his hand on it and presses.

"Sluice footing's rock. Frame's bolted in it." He doesn't raise his voice to Bram, but it reaches the top. "That gap's no place to step over. I stay this side. Low." He stretches out flat on his belly, with the rope across his back running up to the rail-post. Lying like that, his weight is as far from the edge as he can get it.

Sefa asks about lowering Pell to a proper floor, and Osric gives her a short look across the hole.

"He's on the floor."

Then he jerks his head at the water, at the black deck-beam lying half-sunk across the corner of the chamber.

"Beam goes under the block. Low edge, rough side. Rope round the far end, up to the lip. Two haul, the beam lifts, block tips off him." He breathes in through his nose. "Shifted blocks forty years. Comes up easy with the beam. Sits there a week without it."

Sefa's light shows her what Osric is describing. The block lies tilted with its carved face up: a sun disc with straight rays and a ring of small cut marks around it. It's the sunburst that Lathander's people cut over their doors and on their altar-cloths, cut here into a stone at the bottom of a quarry. The jagged lower edge has gone into the water, and the leg is under it. A hospice novice has seen this kind of wound on the docks, when a cargo net gave way. The stone has bitten in and is holding the torn flesh shut by its own weight. While the block stays put, the leg won't bleed much. Once it lifts, the wound will open and bleed hard, all at once. Whoever lifts it needs healing ready at that same moment: a potion down his throat, or her light on him.

The wall behind the block, where it once stood, shows a square patch of old grey plaster. Every surface in the working is wet: the cut stone, the pink tidemark, the rotten wood. The plaster is the only thing down there that looks dry.

The seep keeps trickling from the crack in the far wall, and the water has risen a hair's breadth against the tidemark.

 Sefa holds the stone low over the lip, angled so its light falls on the face below her and leaves the water dark. She talks down to him the whole time, unhurried and steady. When she asked about an anchor, Bram's half-hitch on the rail-post had already answered her: that post holds the warden's line now. Osric answered the rest flat: there's nowhere lower to put a man than the bottom. Her offer of warmth goes down the shaft with her voice and stays offered. The Lantern's light sits ready in her hands, unspent.

Up at the head of the walk, Bram keeps the silk line steady in his left hand. It's taut and he isn't hauling, so nothing pulls the pinned leg against the stone.
>>>

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gets his chin up and both hands flat on the block's carved face, bracing his weight off the leg so he doesn't grind it further. He doesn't try to shift it. He breathes slow and shallow through the wet rag and keeps his eyes open on purpose, fixed on the grey shaft of light.

Up the hole, loud and clear, so the walk can hear: "I'm all right! Leg's pinned, not broken! Listen, because this matters." He forces the words out evenly. "Stone's holding a cut shut. When it lifts, I bleed bad. My pack's at the head of the walk. Potions are in the side pocket, three of 'em. Bram, get one down to Osric on the line before anyone touches this block. Sefa, you be ready too. Whoever's closest when it shifts, pour."

Then, quieter, to Osric at the lip: "I'll keep talking, warden. You tell me if I start making less sense than usual."

While he waits, he works one-handed under the water. He pulls the belt off his waist, gets it round his left thigh above the knee, and cinches it hard. He knots it so it holds and twists a dagger-hilt through it as a windlass if it'll take one. A Lower City surgeon showed him that once on a man with a broken bottle in his leg. "Strap's on above the knee," he calls up. "That buys us a few breaths when it comes off."

He looks at the half-sunk deck-beam across the corner, measuring it. "There's a beam down here, still whole. If you drop me a second line, I'll loop it round the end and you haul it up for a lever. Wedge it under the block's top edge from the lip and pry *toward the wall*, not toward me. Don't let it roll back onto the leg." He grits his teeth through a shiver. "Count it off before you heave. I want to know when."

Then, because he has to keep talking anyway, he squints at the carving under his palms. "Osric, there's a sun cut on this stone. Disc, straight rays, ring of little marks round it like a tally. And plaster behind where it stood. Anybody ever say what this place was before it was a quarry?"

? Two things. First: I shrugged off my pack at the head of the walk last round, and the potions were in it, so I'm assuming they're up top, not on me. Correct me if I'm wrong. Second: I'm holding Sefa's Guidance in reserve for whatever check the air or the cold throws at me, unless a roll comes up for something else first.

scenes.narration:
Pell gets his chin up and sets both palms flat on the carved face of the block, taking his weight off the leg. The stone is cold and gritty with wet chalk under his hands. He breathes through the wet rag in short, even pulls and keeps his eyes on the grey shaft of light coming down through the hole.

His voice goes up the shaft loud and level, and it carries off the walls of the cut. Osric is flat on his belly at the lip and doesn't interrupt. When Pell gets to the pack and the side pocket, the warden lifts his head and looks up the walk to the head of the cut, where the pack lies on the stone a stride from the sealed box, out in the sun.

"Pack's up top. By the box." He fills his chest and bellows up the walk, louder than Pell has heard him yet: "Flask! Side pocket of his pack! Down on the line to me! Nobody touches the block till it's here!" Then he lowers his eyes to Pell again.

To the quieter thing Pell said to him, Osric gives the hole a long, flat look. "Hard to tell."

Under the water Pell gets to work one-handed. He hauls the belt out of its loops, feeds it round his left thigh above the knee and draws it in. His fingers have gone stupid with cold. Twisting a dagger-hilt through a strap is a trick he has seen done once, by a back-alley surgeon on a dry floor, and never by a man chest-deep in cold water.

The belt goes round and the buckle bites, but the leather is soaked and stretches as fast as he pulls it. When he works a dagger-hilt through the strap and turns it, the wet leather turns with it. The hilt spins loose and the strap slides back as slack as it went on. It's round his thigh and it isn't holding anything. Pell calls up that the strap is on. The warden grunts and lets it go.

He feels something else as his hands come up out of the water. The steady warmth Sefa pressed into his wrist before he went down has gone. The cold seems to have washed it out of him somewhere between the ledge and the bottom, and there's nothing left in his fingers but the ache.

When Pell talks about the beam, Osric turns his head and looks along the chamber at it for a long moment, measuring it the way he measures blocks.

"Low edge. Rough side. Tip goes under." He says it to the water, then to Pell. "Toward the wall, yes. She falls that way anyhow. Weight's on the wall side." He breathes in through his nose. "Count it off. Three, then heave. You'll hear it."

There's no second line down here. Osric settles that himself. He gets one hand round an iron spoke of the sluice-wheel, drags the hempen loop off over his head with the other, and lies there on the bolted rock with nothing tying him to anything. Above him the line still runs taut to Bram's half-hitch on the rail-post. He pays out the slack hand over hand and lowers the end down the shaft. It splashes into the black water an arm's length from the near end of the beam.

Pell stretches until the pinned leg protests, gets the end under his fingers and takes it twice round the timber with a knot he could tie in his sleep. Osric draws the slack up and leans his weight back. The beam comes out of the corner reluctantly, streaming water and black rot. He walks it in until its butt rises against the broken lip of the hole and its tip hangs in the water a foot from the jagged edge of the block. He holds it there without letting it go any closer.

"Not yet." He wedges the rope under the sluice-frame's foot. "Not till the flask's in my hand."

Then he looks down at the carving under Pell's palms, at the disc and the rays and the small marks running round it like a tally. He looks for a long time. Plainly he has never seen it before in his life.

"Thirty years. Never knew that was there." He doesn't look away from it. "Always a quarry. Long as there's been a Beregost." A pause. "Old men said the Song's first stones came out of this hill. Temple's. Lathander's lot." He looks at the patch of grey plaster on the wall, the one dry thing in the room, and says nothing about it.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, can you get a rope round that beam without putting your head under? Don’t try if you can’t.”

I secure Pell’s silk line to the tested post, keeping its tension unchanged, then go down the sound planks to Sefa.

“Osric, can you secure your line to the sluice-frame instead? That gives us the free end for the beam. Keep yourself tied.”

I stay on the last sound planks. If we can get the hempen line round the beam, I take the hauling end alongside Sefa.

“Tell us when it’s placed. We lift slowly on your word, Osric. Pell, tell us the moment your leg’s clear—we’ll hold it while you move.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa braces her back against the rail and lets the light fall full on Pell's upturned face. When she speaks, her voice reaches down the shaft the way a bell carries over water.

"Pell, listen to me. The moment that block comes off, the leg is going to pour. I know it, and Osric knows it. That's not the wound to flinch from — it's the one we're going to meet together. Here's the order."

She glances at Osric, then Bram. "Set the beam. Bind the rope round its far end and up over the lip, so two can haul from where the footing holds. Bram keeps the line, no slack, though the stones themselves start climbing. Osric, you take the beam and call when it's set. On my word, lift."

She shifts her grip, the lit stone steady in her other hand. "I'll pour the Lantern's light into him at the same instant the weight goes off the leg — four dice of it, no skimping. And whoever can reach him first puts both hands on the wound and kneels on it, if there's a knee to spare. You press until I tell you to ease."

Her eyes drop once to the carved sun-disc, and something in her voice rounds with recognition. "That's Lathander's sun on that block. His shrine was down here once, holding back the dark and the seep. It didn't fall on you to bury you, Pell."

Then, to Osric: "When the beam's set and everyone's braced, call it. I'll give the count."

scenes.narration:
Bram ties the silk line off before he lets go of it. He takes two turns round the tested rail-post, below the half-hitch on the hempen line, and finishes with a hitch of his own. When he takes his hand away the silk stays exactly as taut as it was, and nothing shifts at the other end. Then he goes down the switchbacks plank by plank and stops on the last sound tread beside Sefa. His shield arm brushes the rail as he comes.

From there both of them can see what Osric has done. The hempen line runs from the post above them, down along the rail, over the broken lip and into the hole, and it's already tied twice round the old deck-beam. The beam leans up out of the water with its butt against the rotten edge and its tip hanging a foot short of the block's rough lower side. The beam is set and roped, and the rope Bram was going to ask for is already on it.

Sefa's voice goes down the shaft, and Osric lies flat on the sluice side and listens to all of it. When she says *Lantern's light* and *four dice*, he turns his head and looks at the stone glowing in her hand. He looks at it the same way he looked at the beam, judging what weight it can bear.

He answers Bram first.

"Can't." He lifts the hand that's holding the sluice-wheel just long enough to point at the rope. "That's the lever now. Can't be my line and the beam's too." He grips the iron spoke again. "Frame's bolted in rock. I hold that."

Then he looks down at the rope where it crosses the lip, and up at the run of it along the rail, an arm's length from Bram's boots.

"You and me haul. You on the rope there, me on the butt from this side. Tip goes under the low edge, the rough one. She tips to the wall." He looks at Sefa. "You don't haul. You do your light."

When Sefa says the sun on the block is Lathander's, Osric doesn't argue. His eyes go to the square of grey plaster on the wall behind it, and they stay there a moment longer than they need to. He doesn't say anything about it, the same as before.

"Your count, then," he says to her.

Then he looks past both of them, up the switchbacks to the head of the walk. Pell's pack lies there on the white stone in the sun, a stride from the sealed case, with the side pocket still buckled. Bram has come down without it.

"Flask's still up there." He says it flat, as plain fact. "Light's good. I seen your stone." He works his jaw. "Flask's what I know. Wanted it in my hand before we heave."

He puts his free hand on the butt of the beam and leaves it there without pushing yet. The seep goes on trickling from the crack in the far wall, and down in the grey shaft of light the water stands a little higher against the pink tidemark.

 These four didn't need rolls, so here is why each one went the way it did:

1) Bram ties Pell's silk line off on the post. That's ordinary rope work on an anchor he had already tested, so nothing was uncertain. It's tied, and the tension on it is the same as before.
2) Bram walks down to Sefa on planks that are known to hold. It's plain movement, and he's now on the last sound plank beside her.
3) Osric securing his line to the sluice-frame was Bram asking Osric, not something Bram does himself. Osric turned him down aloud and gave his reason: the hempen line is the lever now, so it can't also be his safety line. He holds the bolted sluice-wheel instead, and he's still untied. It's up to Bram's player whether Bram answers that next round.
4) This was Bram's action, not Osric's. The condition he set is met, because the hempen line is already round the beam. Bram takes hold of it where it runs along the rail beside the last plank, next to Sefa, ready to haul. The heave itself hasn't happened yet. It waits for Sefa's count, and Osric has said aloud that he wants a flask in his hand first. When the heave comes, it will be rolled then.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell spits a mouthful of chalky water past the rag and calls up straight away, because a lie about this kills him.

"Warden, correction. The strap's no good. Wet leather's stretched and the twist won't hold. Count it as nothing." He gets the heel of his hand under the water, finds the soft hollow high on the inside of his left thigh, and leans his weight into it, hard, the way you'd hold a door shut. "Holding it with my hand instead. Better than nothing, not much."

He jerks his chin at the pink tidemark. "And the water's coming up. Slow, but it's coming. That crack's feeding it, so we don't wait any longer than we have to."

Then louder, up the shaft to Bram and Sefa: "Flask comes to *me*, not to Osric! Bram, tie it in a loop of cord round my silk line and let it slide down. The line runs straight to me. I'll hold it uncorked, and the moment the stone shifts it's down my throat. Quicker than anyone can reach me." He takes a breath. "Sefa, after the heave, you're the second shot. If I'm still bleeding, bring your light."

To Osric, between clenched teeth: "When the flask's in my hand, you count three and heave toward the wall. Don't stop for me shouting. I'll be shouting."

His eyelids drag again. He bites the inside of his cheek hard enough to taste copper, scoops cold water over his face with his free hand, and keeps talking just to keep talking. "Lathander's lot, you said. First stones of the Song. So somebody sealed a sun in this wall and plastered behind it." He squints at the grey patch. "That's not a quarry thing. That's someone hiding a door. We'll look at it after I've got two legs, eh?"

He keeps his eyes open on the grey light and holds his free hand up out of the water, ready to catch the flask.

? Understood on the Guidance. It ran out while I was down here, no argument. I'll take on the tourniquet failure. I'm keeping my last reroll.

scenes.narration:
Pell spits a mouthful of chalk-water past the rag, and his voice goes up the shaft flat and plain. Osric takes the correction about the strap without blinking.

"Heard. Strap's nothing."

Under the water Pell finds the hollow high on the inside of his thigh, where the pulse sits close under the skin, and leans the heel of his hand into it. The cold has numbed the leg so much that he can't tell how much good it's doing. For now the stone is still doing most of the work, and he knows it.

The warden turns his head when Pell nods at the tidemark. He looks along the pink crust to the crack in the far wall, where the trickle comes through thin and steady, and back again. He doesn't argue with any of it.

Pell shouts up about the flask: tie it round the silk line, slide it down, straight to him. Osric listens through to the end. Then he looks at the silk line where it runs taut up through the hole, a hand's breadth from Pell's raised fingers, and he works out the reason as he would work out a load.

"Your line. Runs to you." A short pause. "Your throat. Quicker." He fills his chest and sends it up the walk after Pell's shout, louder and rougher: "Flask down *his* line! Not mine! To him!" Then he settles back on his belly with one hand on the wheel-spoke and the other on the butt of the beam.

To the quieter part he gives a single nod. "Flask in your hand. Three. Heave to the wall." His eyes stay on Pell's face. "You shout. I don't stop."

Pell's eyelids drag again, slower this time, like a curtain somebody is drawing on purpose. He bites the inside of his cheek until he tastes copper and throws a palmful of cold water over his face. The cold jerks him awake, and he keeps talking.

When he says *hiding a door*, Osric's eyes go to the grey plaster and stay on it. A drop of seep runs down the cut stone beside it, darkening the stone as it goes. It reaches the edge of the plaster and goes around it, as if the plaster weren't wet at all.

"After." That's all he says.

Grey light comes down the shaft onto Pell's upturned face and his free hand, held up out of the water. Somewhere above, at the head of the walk, the pack lies in the sun beside the sealed case. The trickle keeps coming through the crack in the far wall. The water has crept up the pink tidemark again, by about the thickness of a fingernail, since Pell first saw it.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa draws a long breath and lets it out slow. Every line in her body settles into the plank — not braced to run, but braced to act.

"All right," she says, and her voice is calm as a bell at night. "Pell, stay awake. Look at the light. On three, say when you're clear. Don't try to pull free; let them lift the stone off you, not the leg out from under it."

She holds the glowing stone out over the hole, so its light falls steady on his face and on the beam and the black water below. Her free hand comes up, open, as if she's about to catch something falling toward her.

"Ready at the beam?" she calls to Osric. "Rope?" to Bram.

Then she counts, slow and even, so there is no mistaking it:

"One. Take the strain."

The rope creaks. She watches the beam's tip shift against the block's rough lower edge.
