scenes.narration:
Sefa's voice carries down the shaft, calm and unhurried. The stone's light holds steady on the water and on the black deck-beam where it leans against the broken lip. Her free hand comes up open over the hole.

Bram answers her before she reaches *one*.

"Hold the lift. I'll fetch it."

He's already turning. He goes back up the switchbacks at a brisk walk, testing each tread out of habit even at that pace, and his shield knocks once against the rail at the turn. Sefa's count goes on behind him, slow and even, bouncing off the stained walls.

"One. Take the strain."

Osric's hand stays flat on the butt of the beam. He doesn't push.

"Two."

The hempen line lies along the rail with nobody on it. It's still tied off at the post and hasn't moved.

"Three. Lift."

Nothing moves. Osric lies on his belly on the bolted rock with his palm on the timber and his other fist round the wheel-spoke. The beam's tip hangs a foot short of the block's rough edge, exactly where he left it. The stone doesn't shift. The light Sefa has been holding stays where it is, waiting behind her ribs for a moment that hasn't come.

"Not yet," Osric says across the hole, without heat.

At the head of the walk the sun lies white on the stone. Pell's pack sits a stride from the sealed case, and Bram crouches over it and works the buckle of the side pocket open. Three red flasks are packed in rag, side by side. He takes one out.

"Pell! Taking a potion from your satchel!" The shout goes down the cut and comes back off the walls.

He goes down again with the flask in his fist, plank by plank, until he's back on the last sound tread beside Sefa. From there he can see what he'd have to do to put it in Osric's hand. He'd have to cross the open hole or the rotten skin around it, with the warden flat on the far side. He doesn't try it. He stands the flask on the plank at Sefa's feet, wedged against the foot of the rail where a stray boot won't send it over. Then he takes the hempen line in both hands where it runs along the rail, sets his heels on the sound planking and takes up the slack until the rope tightens.

"Ready. Slow lift on Sefa's count."

Osric lifts his head and looks at the red flask standing on the plank, then down the shaft. He breathes in through the wet rag.

"That's up there." His eyes go to the silk line, which runs taut from the post above them, past the rail and down through the hole. "His line's right by you. Flask goes down that. Into his hand. Then three." He settles his palm back on the butt of the beam. "Not before."

Bram's line is tight across the lip. The light falls steady into the shaft. A drop of seep runs down the wall of the working, reaches the grey plaster and goes around it. In the crack in the far wall the trickle keeps coming, and the water has crept another fingernail's breadth up the pink tidemark.

 (Out of game: here's why none of these four needed a roll.)
1) Sefa set her Healing Light to go off the moment the stone shifts. The stone never moved, so the light hasn't been spent.
2) Sefa's count is just her speaking, so nothing to roll. Osric said aloud why he held the heave: the flask has to be in Pell's hand first. So no lift happened to roll.
3) Bram taking a flask out of an unlocked side pocket is routine. He has it, and it's now standing on the plank at Sefa's feet.
4) Bram bracing on the rope is just him getting into position. The heave gets rolled when someone actually tries it.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his free hand high on the silk line where it runs taut above his fingers, watching for the flask to come sliding down out of the grey light. His other hand stays buried at his thigh, leaning into the pulse point.

When it reaches him, he closes his fist round it, gets the cork between his back teeth through a fold of the rag and pulls it, and spits the cork into the water. He holds the open flask against his chest, upright, just under his chin, so nothing slops out when the block goes.

"Got it! Flask's in my hand, cork's out!" he calls up the shaft, loud enough for the walk to hear too. "Sefa, Bram, we're heaving now. Be ready on the line. If I go under, haul me up the second the stone's clear, block or no block."

Then he looks up at Osric, steady, and draws one slow breath through the wet cloth.

"Right, warden. Your count."

He braces his good foot against the chamber floor so he can shove himself away from the block the instant it lifts, and he keeps the heel of his hand hard on the inside of his thigh. The moment he feels the weight come off, he means to tip the flask down his throat. He won't stop to look at the leg first.

"And Osric," he adds through his teeth, "if it rolls back toward me, let it fall. Don't try to catch it."

? Two things. The records show my potions reshuffled: one listed separately, two together. Is that one now in my hand, slid down the silk line? I've written this round as if the flask has reached me. If it hasn't, read it as Pell waiting with his hand up and calling the count only once it arrives. Also, drinking it is a bonus action by the campaign rules, with Fast Hands too. I want it to go down the same instant the block shifts, before the bleeding takes hold.

scenes.narration:
Pell keeps his free hand up on the silk line where it runs taut a hand's breadth above his fingers. He watches the grey light at the top of the shaft for anything sliding down it. His other hand stays under the water, the heel of it pressed hard into the hollow high on his thigh. He sets his good foot against the floor of the working, behind and to one side, so that he can shove himself away from the block when it moves.

Nothing comes down the line.

Looking straight up the shaft past the broken lip, he can see the underside of the last sound plank. Sefa's stone glows there, steady and white, and beside the foot of the rail is a small red glint, a flask standing upright on the wood. It's still up there, not on the line, and not in his hand. The silk runs past it, taut and empty.

Osric is flat on his belly on the sluice side, one fist round the wheel-spoke and his palm on the butt of the beam. He follows Pell's eyes up the shaft to the red glint and back down. He doesn't push.

When Pell speaks through his teeth about letting the stone fall, the warden gives a short nod.

"Let it fall. Not catching a block." His eyes stay on Pell's face. "Done that once. Young. Cost two fingers." He doesn't show which hand. "Flask first. Then three."

The beam stays where he holds it. Its rotten tip hangs a foot short of the block's rough lower edge, and water drips off it into the black surface.

The cold goes on working into Pell. His teeth ache with it, and his raised arm starts to burn from holding still. The sweetness under the wet rag hasn't gone anywhere. Somewhere in the waiting his eyelids drag again, slower than before, and he only notices because the grey light at the top of the shaft has dimmed for a moment. Then the ache in his teeth brings him back to it. The light is bright again, the flask is still standing on the plank, and the silk line is still empty above his fingers.

The trickle keeps coming through the crack in the far wall. The pink tidemark is that much nearer the water.

 (Out of game: Pell hasn't drunk the flask because it's still standing on the plank, not in his hand, and the block hasn't been lifted. The drink happens as a bonus action, with no roll needed, the moment both are true.)

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, flask coming down your line. Can you catch and hold it?”

I keep the hauling rope steady. “Sefa, use the wrapping rag to sling the flask onto his silk line and slide it down to his hand. Keep your light on him.”

I stay braced, taking the beam’s weight without lifting yet.

“Once he has it, give us a fresh count. Osric, call a halt if the beam slips. We lift only far enough to free his leg.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa looks at the taut silk line, then down the shaft to Pell. "Flask goes down the easy way," she says. "We let no slack into that line, and I won't tie a knot on it with a man below."

She tucks the glowing stone into the crook of her arm, bright side out over the hole, and makes a small shaping gesture with her free hand. A spectral hand winks into being near the red flask at her feet — little more than a heat-shimmer in the daylight. It takes the neck of the flask lightly, lifts it clear of the rail, and carries it out over the shaft, then down, lowering it hand over hand toward Pell's upturned palm.

"Pell, give me your hand where I can see it," she calls. "Take it, but don't drink it yet. Keep it stoppered in your fist. Drink when the weight leaves your leg and I say the word — not before, or the healing passes through you while the blood's still held."

She watches the spectral hand descend, steady as a nurse lowering a basin into a ward cot. "Bram, stay snug on the hauling line. Osric, the call's on me as soon as he has it. Then we lift."

She lets out a breath.

"Pell, when it's in your hand, say so."

scenes.narration:
Bram keeps both hands on the hempen line, heels set on the sound planking, and holds the rope taut so the beam's weight sits in his arms without lifting. His voice goes down the shaft loud and even.

Sefa doesn't reach for the rag. She tucks the glowing stone into the crook of her arm, bright side out over the hole. With her free hand she makes a small shaping motion over the red flask at her feet. Something takes hold of the flask's neck, little more than a shimmer in the daylight, like heat coming off a summer roof. It lifts the flask clear of the rail-foot and carries it out over the broken lip, then starts down the shaft. The silk line stays as taut as Bram left it, and nothing slides along it or touches it.

Osric turns his head on the bolted rock and watches the flask go down. The red glass catches Sefa's light at every hand's breadth of the drop: past the jagged rim of rotten timber, past the pink ribbons on the walls, and into the grey shaft where Pell's free hand is raised out of the water. The shimmer stops a finger's width above his palm and holds the flask there, upright and still.

Osric looks back up at Bram when he hears *call a halt if the beam slips*.

"Slips, I shout." He shifts his palm on the butt of the timber and spreads his fingers. "Can't lift her half. Tip goes under, she tips to the wall or she don't." His eyes go to Sefa. "Your count. When it's his."

Bram's rope creaks once under the strain and goes quiet. The beam's rotten tip hangs a foot short of the block's rough lower edge, dripping into the black water. Down by the far wall the seep keeps trickling through its crack, and the water has crept a little further up the pink tidemark.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell sees the red glint on the plank and swears softly into the rag. Then he fills his lungs and shouts up the shaft, slow and clear so nobody can mishear him:

"Flask's on the bottom plank! By the rail foot! It's standing there, it's not on the line! Whoever's nearest, *tie it to the silk and let it slide*. Cord, bootlace, anything. Loop it round the line and let go. It'll find me."

He gives the silk line three sharp tugs, so whoever holds the anchor end feels it in their hands.

Then, lower, to Osric, without taking his eyes off the glint: "Warden. Can you reach it from where you lie, without leaving good rock? If you can, just drop it down the shaft to me. I'll catch it, I've caught worse falling off roofs." A breath. "If you can't, don't stretch for it. I'm not worth your two other fingers."

He shifts his raised arm to rest the wrist against the silk so it stops burning, and keeps the heel of his other hand hard in his thigh.

"And tell them up top I'm going slow," he adds, quieter, honest about it. "The air's getting at me. Lights went dim on me just now. If I stop talking, that's not me being sulky. Haul."

He keeps his eyes open on the red glint and starts counting under his breath, one, two, three, over and over, just to have something to hold on to.

scenes.narration:
Pell swears into the wet rag, low and short. Then he fills his chest and sends it up the shaft slowly, one word at a time, so the cut can't throw it back garbled: *flask on the bottom plank, by the rail foot, tie it to the silk and let it slide.* The walls give it back to him twice over.

He gives the silk line three hard tugs. It doesn't give at all. It runs straight up through the hole, as stiff as a bar, and doesn't twitch the way a rope does in a man's fist. That isn't a hand at the other end. It's a knot on a post.

Osric hears the question put to him and doesn't move off the rock to answer it.

"Can't. Hole's between." His palm stays spread on the butt of the beam. When Pell tells him he isn't worth the other two fingers, the warden's eyes don't leave Pell's face. "Got eight. Not spending 'em on you."

Then he looks up. So does Pell.

The red glint isn't on the plank any more. It's coming down the shaft, past the jagged rim of rotten timber and the pink ribbons glittering wet on the walls. It hangs upright in the empty air a good arm's length from the silk line and touches nothing. Something holds it by the neck, a faint ripple in the grey light, like the air over a summer roof. It drops steadily, a hand's breadth at a time, and stops a finger's width above Pell's raised palm. It stays there, the red glass catching Sefa's light.

Osric watches it hang there and says nothing about how it got there. When Pell asks him to pass word up the walk, he does, and he says it the way Pell said it. "He's slow! Air's at him! He stops talking, you haul!" His voice comes off the walls rough, then he turns back down to the hole. "Heard you. Keep counting."

Pell rests his wrist against the silk. The burn in his raised arm eases. The heel of his other hand stays buried in the hollow of his thigh, and he can no longer feel the leg below it. He counts under his breath, *one, two, three*, the same three over and over.

The shimmer holding the flask wavers once, the way heat-haze breaks up when a cloud crosses the sun. The red glass dips a hair toward his palm, then steadies. Above, the beam's rotten tip still hangs a foot short of the block's rough edge, dripping into the black water. At the far wall the seep keeps coming through its crack, and the pink tidemark is that much closer to the surface.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps the spectral hand steady as she speaks, without hurry.

"Close your fingers now, Pell. It's coming the last inch into your palm." The red flask settles into his hand, and she waits a breath for his fingers to close. "Don't drink yet. Say when you've got it — and keep it in your fist."

When his confirmation comes back up the shaft, she turns her head just enough for Bram and Osric to hear.

"Fresh count, then. On three the stone comes off. At the same moment I pour the Lantern's light into him, and Pell drinks. Then we clamp that leg, and no one eases until I say so."

She keeps her eyes moving — Pell's free hand, the beam, the rope, the water creeping at the tidemark.

"For now, just tell me you have it."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Understood. Tip her to the wall.”

I keep my footing and the rope taut, watching the beam. Once Pell has the flask and Sefa gives her count, I haul steadily with both hands, working with Osric to bring the tip under the block and overturn it against the wall.

I hold the strain until Osric says the block is settled.

scenes.narration:
Sefa doesn't hurry the hand. She lowers the shimmer the last finger's width, and the red flask settles upright into the cup of Pell's raised palm. Glass meets skin. From the last plank she sees the glint come to rest on his hand, and a breath later the ripple in the grey light thins out and is gone. The cantrip has run its minute. Nothing holds the flask now except the hand it is sitting in.

Her voice goes down the shaft unhurried: close your fingers, don't drink yet, say when you have it.

While she speaks, the sounds from below catch up with the people at the top. Pell's earlier shout comes up the shaft slow and clear, *flask on the bottom plank, tie it to the silk*. It is out of date now, the flask long past the plank. Then the silk line twitches at the rail-post, three short jerks against Bram's hitch. The knot takes them without giving, and the line stays as stiff as before. Then Osric's voice comes off the walls, rougher than any of theirs:

"He's slow! Air's at him! He stops talking, you haul!"

Under it, faint enough that Sefa has to lean over the lip to be sure of it, a low counting rises from the water: *one, two, three*, and then the same three again.

Bram doesn't answer with words. He sets his heels a little wider on the sound planking, takes another inch of slack out of the hempen line and holds it there. The beam's weight sits in his arms, and the rope runs tight along the rail and over the broken lip. Nothing lifts yet. "Understood. Tip her to the wall," he says, and keeps his eyes on the rotten tip of the timber where it hangs over the block's rough edge.

Osric hears Sefa's fresh count laid out, three, light, drink, and he doesn't argue with the order of it. When she says *clamp that leg*, he lifts his head off the rock and looks down the shaft, then at the eight feet of open air between the lip and the water.

"Nobody down there to clamp." He doesn't say it to argue. He says it flatly, the way he'd point out that a load was too long for a cart. "His own hand. And your light." He settles his palm back on the butt of the beam and spreads his fingers on the wet wood. "He says *got it*, you count."

Below, the red glass sits on Pell's raised palm in the grey light. The counting goes on under it, and Sefa's stone shines on all of it. Across the working the seep keeps trickling through the crack in the far wall, and the black water has crept a little further up the pink tidemark.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't snatch, because snatching knocks things away. He closes his fingers slowly round the neck of the flask, just under the shimmer, and feels the weight settle into his hand.

"Got it. Whoever that is, thank you." He gets the cork between his back teeth through a fold of the rag, pulls, and spits it into the water. He holds the open flask upright against his chest, just under his chin.

Then he shouts up the shaft, slower now, because the words want to slur: "Flask's in my hand! Cork's out! And listen, my silk's tied off on a post, nobody's holding it. Somebody take it in hand *now*. If I go under, a post can't haul me."

He waits a breath to see whether the line twitches and changes from a bar into a rope.

He sets his good foot against the floor again, keeps the heel of his hand buried in his thigh, and looks up at Osric.

"Your count, warden. Three, heave to the wall. I drink the moment it moves." His eyes drag. He bites his cheek again, tastes copper, and blinks hard. "Go."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“He’s fading. We lift now. Sefa, give him your light when the stone moves.”

I call down, “Pell! Hold that flask. We’re getting the weight off.”

“Osric—one, two, THREE.”

On three I haul hard and steadily, putting my legs and back into the rope while Osric guides the beam beneath the block. I keep hauling to tip the stone against the wall, not stopping halfway.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa leans over the lip a little further, close enough that her voice goes down into the hole as well as across it.

"Pell! Say the word and call back. We don't lift until I hear your voice — not a twitch of the rope, your voice."

Then, because the counting from the water has planted itself in the base of her skull and will not be ignored, she begins to speak in time with it, a low, steady cadence that follows the shaft down through the dark — the old field-chant nurses use to time compressions, matching it deliberately to the rhythm below:

"Stay with the light. Stay with the light. Stay with the light."

It isn't panic. It's a toehold. Her hand with the stone never wavers. Her eyes move along the black water's edge, searching where the counting comes from, but her voice stays even, and her count stays for Pell.

scenes.narration:
Pell's voice reaches the top of the shaft before Bram has finished bracing. It comes up hoarse and slow: *flask's in my hand, cork's out*. Then something about the silk line and a post that can't haul. Osric's bellow follows it up the walk, rougher and shorter: "He's got it! *Count!*"

Sefa leans out over the lip and asks for Pell's voice, and she has already heard it. Under the shouting the low counting from the water starts again. She takes it up and lays her own words over its beat, *stay with the light*, steady and unhurried, a nurse timing a ward. The stone in her hand doesn't waver.

Bram doesn't wait for anyone else's count. He holds the rope, and Osric settled that a lift goes on the voice of whoever holds it. Bram calls down the shaft to Pell, sets his heels, and counts.

"One. Two. *Three.*"

The Lantern's light goes down through the grey shaft like sun through a high window. It isn't the white of the stone in her hand. It's warmer, the colour of a lamp turned up in a dark ward, and it settles on the water where Pell is. Sefa sees the black water darken around him as the torn leg opens, a cloud spreading out from under the surface. Then it stops spreading. Whatever the Lantern sent has met the wound and closed it as fast as it opened, and more than closed it.

As the light goes down, the square of old grey plaster on the wall flushes with it for a heartbeat. The wet cut stone around it only reflects the light. The plaster seems to take it in, the way milk-glass holds a candle, and it goes on glowing faintly for a breath after the rest of the working has gone grey again. Then it's only plaster.

Osric is still flat on the sluice-side rock with the beam butt under his shoulder. He lets go of it slowly, the way a man lets go of something heavy that might shift again. He looks at the block lying face to the wall, then down at the water, then up the shaft at Sefa. His mouth opens and shuts again before anything comes out.

"Off him." He breathes in hard through the wet rag. "Off."

The hempen line hangs slack along the rail in Bram's hands. Pell's silk still runs straight and stiff from the post down into the hole. The black water slaps once more against the walls of the working, settles, and goes still. At the far wall the seep keeps trickling through its crack.

 The light Sefa sent down is more than the wound needed. The leg could have opened right to the bone and the Lantern would still have had enough to close it. What reaches Pell in the water is everything the fall and the stone took out of him: the bruises from the drop, the bitten shin, the ache the cold had driven into him. All of it is put back. From the lip of the hole she can see the warmth settle on him and stay there, and the dark cloud in the water around him has stopped spreading.

scenes.narration:
Pell bites his cheek hard enough to taste copper. He presses the open flask flat against his breastbone with his thumb over the mouth, and his voice goes up the shaft hoarse but steady. Osric hears what he says about staying out of his way and nods once, without taking his eyes off the beam.

The count that comes down the shaft is Bram's, not Sefa's: *one*, booming off the stained walls, then *two*. Under it Sefa's voice keeps a slower beat, *stay with the light*, steady as a ward clock. Pell mouths the numbers along with Bram. On *three* the hempen line jerks taut over the lip. Osric gets his shoulder in behind the butt of the beam and grunts, and the rotten tip drives down under the block's rough lower edge.

The weight comes off Pell's leg all at once.

He tips the flask back as he feels it go and gets it down in one swallow. The potion is warm and thick, and it tastes of iron. With the good foot he shoves himself back through the water towards Osric's side. Behind him the block goes over with a slow, heavy roll. It lands face to the wall with a crack that he feels through the floor of the working, and a wave slaps across the chamber.

Then the leg opens. Pell feels the heat of it before any pain, and the water around his thigh turns black.

Light comes down the shaft. It's warmer than the white glow of Sefa's stone, the colour of a lamp turned up in a dark room, and it settles on him in the water and stays. The heat in the leg stops, then turns into something like sun on cold skin. The ache the drop left in his hip and shoulder goes, and so does the bitten shin. The cold that had got into his teeth lets go of them too. When he puts his free hand down to his thigh there's no wound under his fingers, only torn cloth over smooth skin. The cloud in the water stops spreading and begins to thin. The potion's warmth is still in his chest, with nothing left for it to do.

From down here Pell sees something the others can only see from above. As the light falls into the working, the square of old grey plaster on the wall, an arm's length from him, takes it in. It doesn't shine back like wet stone. It flushes like milk-glass with a candle behind it and goes on glowing faintly for a breath after the rest of the chamber has gone grey. Then it's plaster again, dry and dull, with the seep running around its edges.

"Haul!" Pell gets it out, and it comes up the shaft in a whole voice.

The silk line runs straight up from his chest through the hole. It's still stiff as a bar, and nothing pulls on it.

Osric lies flat on the sluice-side rock with his palm still on the butt of the beam. He lets go of it slowly, finger by finger, like a man who doesn't trust a stone to stay where it has fallen. He looks at the block lying against the wall, then at Pell standing free in the water, and then up the shaft towards the light. His mouth opens and closes again.

"Off him." He breathes in hard through the wet rag. "Off."

The water settles against the walls of the working. The pink tidemark glitters a hand above the surface, and the sweet smell is still there under everything, faint and patient. At the far wall the seep goes on trickling through its crack.

*(Out of game: it wasn't a slip. Bram's heave and Sefa's light landed in their scene at this same moment, and your drink went down with them.)*

 *(Out of game: neither needed a roll. Drinking a potion you're already holding takes a bonus action and can't fail, and with the block's weight gone and nothing in the way, pushing back through still water was ordinary movement, so both simply happened as the story tells it.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, we’re hauling you out. Keep your arms clear of the edge.”

I set down the slack hempen line and hurry up the sound planks to the silk line’s anchor. Keeping a firm grip on the loaded rope, I ease the hitch so I can haul, leaving a turn around the post to hold against a slip.

“Sefa, guide him past the broken timbers from the planks. Stay out of the hole.”

I haul Pell steadily towards the lip, taking in the line and securing each gain. If he catches on anything, I stop rather than drag him against it.

scenes.narration:
Bram's voice goes down the shaft first, and it comes back off the stained walls. Then he lays the slack hempen line along the foot of the rail, where it can't tangle round anyone's boots, and climbs. He takes the switchbacks a tread at a time, quickly but still testing each plank, until he's at the first rail-post a stride below the head of the walk. The sun is full on his back there, and the sealed case still sits on its block in the light.

The silk line comes off the post the way he planned it. He holds the loaded part in his right fist and slacks the hitch with his left. He leaves one turn round the post so that if his grip goes, the wood takes the weight before the line can run. The line jumps under his hand once and settles, heavy. A man's weight is on it now, and the post can't hold that for him. It's his to hold.

He hauls. He keeps it slow and even and lets his legs do the work. After each pull he pins the gained line against the post with the turn and takes a fresh grip lower down. The silk is thin and bites into his palms, and it comes in a forearm at a time. Below him the line runs down along the rail and over the broken lip, and he can see the angle of it shift as the weight rises out of the water. Down in the cut there's a heavy wet sound, water falling off cloth and back into the black pool.

Sefa is still on the last sound plank above the hole, holding the stone out over the shaft. Its white light lies steady on the rotten rim and on the silk where it bends over the edge. The low cadence she started there hasn't stopped, *stay with the light*, unhurried, the same beat as before.

Osric hasn't moved off his rock. He's up on his elbows now, watching the line come in over the lip rather than looking into the hole.

"Lip's rotten. Your side." His voice carries up the walk, flat and quick. "Line rides on it, it saws. Slow at the top."

Bram does what he said he'd do. When the line drags against something at the rim, he stops. It isn't a snag on the line itself. It's the drag of weight coming up against an edge that won't take it. He holds what he's gained, with the turn snug round the post and the silk pinned hard. The line hangs taut from his fist, down along the rail and over the broken lip. At the lip a crumb of black rotten timber breaks loose under the strain and patters into the water below.

Nothing else moves for a moment. The light holds on the rim, the weight hangs in Bram's arms, and the seep goes on trickling through its crack in the far wall of the working.

 1) I didn't roll the haul because it wasn't uncertain. A strong man taking in a rope with a turn round a sound post is routine, and Bram did it up to the lip. He stopped there because of the condition he set himself: stop rather than drag if Pell catches on anything. What happens at the rim depends on Pell's own action in his scene.

2) Laying the slack hempen line along the rail is plain handling, so it simply happened.

3) Guiding Pell past the broken timbers is Bram asking Sefa to do it, and Sefa's player hasn't answered yet, so it waits for her next round.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets out a breath that's half a laugh and half a shudder and flexes the leg once under the water. It's whole. He doesn't trust it to stay that way down here.

"Off," he agrees, hoarse. "And out. Before this air finishes what the stone started."

He wades the arm's length to the plaster square anyway. He can't help it. He raps it twice with his knuckles, listening for hollow, and lays his palm flat on it for a single breath to feel whether it's warm, or dry, or anything but plaster. He doesn't scrape or pry. "Glowed when her light hit it," he tells Osric, short. "Not stone. Later. With fresh air and a lamp and nobody sleepy."

Then he takes the silk line in both hands. A rope tied to a post is a rope he can climb. He sets his good feet against the chamber wall and goes up it the way he went up drainpipes above the Wide, hand over hand, fast and steady, past the jagged lip and onto the last sound plank. He keeps to the planking and doesn't put a toe on the bare ledge.

The moment he's up, he crouches, pulls the wet rag off his face and gulps the cleaner air. Then he looks up the walk towards the warm light.

"Sefa. That was you." He touches his thigh through the torn cloth. "I owe you a leg. And whoever walked that flask down on thin air, I owe you a drink." He glances along the walk, curious which of them it was, but doesn't press.

To Osric, still flat on the sluice-side rock: "Warden, come back to the planks the way you went, slow, on the stone you trust. That gate can wait one more minute while we think about how to shut it without anyone standing on bare ledge." A beat, wry. "Whatever the old men said about Lathander's lot, somebody put a sun in your hill and plastered over it. Maela Thorn's buyer might want her salt. The Song of the Morning might want to know about that wall."

He squints up at the sun's height over the rim of the cut, counting the hours back to Beregost, and starts coiling the slack of his silk line.

scenes.narration:
Pell flexes the leg once under the water. The knee bends and the foot answers. Under the torn cloth the skin is smooth, and the leg holds his weight on the floor of the working as if nothing had happened to it.

He wades the arm's length to the plaster square anyway.

He raps on it twice with his knuckles. The cut stone beside it gives back a dead, solid knock. The plaster sounds different: a short, thin, hollow note, like a cupboard door with nothing heavy behind it. He lays his palm flat on it and holds it there for one breath. Everything else down here is wet and cold enough to ache. The plaster is dry under his hand, chalky and fine, and it isn't cold. It's no warmer than a wall a fire was lit against hours ago and has since gone out, and the warmth fades even as he feels it. He doesn't scrape at it or pry.

When he tells Osric the plaster glowed, the warden doesn't take his eyes off it.

"Saw."

That's all he says about it.

Pell takes the silk in both hands and climbs. He sets his feet against the wall of the working and goes up hand over hand. The line above him holds as steady as a drainpipe bolted to brick, and he climbs it at the pace he would climb one. At the top the jagged lip crumbles under his boot. A slab of black rot the size of a bread-board breaks off and slaps into the water below, but his weight is on the rope and not on the rim. He swings a knee over the end of the planking and is on the last sound plank, on wood that holds, with Sefa's stone glowing a stride away. He crouches there dripping and pulls the rag off his face. The air up here still smells of chalk and seep, but nothing sweet sits under it, and it goes down like water after a long run.

His words go up the walk to whoever they're for.

Across the hole, Osric pushes himself up off his elbows onto his knees on the bolted rock when he hears *the way you went*. He looks at the gap between himself and the planks: eight feet of open water and rotten rim, and the place where the ledge used to be.

"Way I went's down there."

He doesn't sound bothered by it. He turns to the sluice-wheel instead, sets both broad hands on the rusted spokes and leans into it. His shoulders bunch under the apron and the wheel doesn't move a hair. He lets go and looks at his palms, red with rust.

"Two hands, I said. Meant two men." He wipes his palms on the apron. "Spare walk-planks. Twelve foot. Stacked back of the tool-shed." He jerks his head up the cut at the yard. "Your key."

Pell talks about the sun in the hill and the Song of the Morning. Osric looks down through the hole at the dark water, where the block lies with its carved face to the wall.

"Temple'd want it back," he says after a while. "Whatever it is." About Thorn's buyer he says nothing at all.

Pell squints up over the rim of the cut. The sun is still climbing and well short of its noon height, and its light lies white across the top of the walk where the pack and the sealed case sit side by side on the stone. Half a day's road to Beregost leaves room before sunset. It doesn't leave room for a long morning here. Pell coils the slack of the silk at his end, wet and heavy in his hands. Below, the cork turns slowly by the far wall, the seep keeps trickling through its crack, and the water creeps up toward the pink tidemark.

 *(Out of game: none of the three needed a roll. Climbing a rope someone is holding is routine for a roof-runner who climbs at full speed. Knocking on plaster and touching it shows what it shows. Feeling a leg that has already been healed carries no uncertainty. All three happened as told.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I hold the line still and secure the gained length to the post before changing my grip.

“Pell, you’re at the lip. Can you get your hands onto the sound planking? Don’t pull on the rotten timber.”

“Sefa, he’s caught at your feet. Set the light down and help guide his shoulders past the edge—from the sound plank. Tell me when he’s clear and I’ll take in more rope.”

I keep the line taut, ready to resume hauling at her call, but don’t drag him harder against the rim.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't take her eyes from the silk where it drags over the rotten lip. She sets her free hand on the line below Bram's fist, not to haul, but to feel what the wood is doing through it.

"Hold a moment, Bram. The line's sawing the edge, and the edge is giving." She shifts along the plank, careful of every inch of footing, until she stands close beside the rail-post. "We need the pull coming up and over something clean. The rail-post, not the lip."

She hooks her elbow around the post to brace herself, then catches the silk below the heavy turn and guides it away from the broken rim, feeding a little sideways pressure hand over hand. It's not strength she's offering; it's direction — the nursing of a thread through a wound.

"Osric," she calls, still in that calm ward-cadence, "is there any iron on the ledge we can put under the rope as a smooth edge? A bar, a stray chisel, even a crushed bucket's handle. And can Pell hug the line and keep clear of the wood on his side?"

She presses her shoulder into the post and holds the rope angled, so the weight bears on sound timber rather than the rotten mouth. "Bram — when you feel it slide clean, pull slow and steady. Don't winch. Don't jerk him up through it."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell straightens up on the plank, wrings the worst of the water out of his sleeves, and nods across the gap.

"Twelve-foot planks, back of the tool-shed. On it." He pats the square keys in his pouch to make sure they came through the swim. "Warden, put Bram's loop back round your chest while you wait. You're sitting on the only good rock left down here, and I've just seen what the rest of it does."

He starts up the walk at a quick, careful trot, staying on the planking, and calls ahead as he climbs:

"Bram! Two planks from the tool-shed. I'll open it, you carry, they'll be heavy. We lay them from the bottom plank across the hole to Osric's rock, side by side, ends lashed so they can't skid. Then I go over and take the other hand on that wheel." He looks back down at the rusted sluice and the rising tidemark. "Two men, two hands each. If it still won't turn, we leave it and he writes *seep* in his book instead of *drowned*."

At the top he spares a glance for the pack and the sealed case in the sun, both still where they were, and a quick, crooked grin for Sefa. "Still owe you a leg." Then he's across the yard to the tool-shed, keys out, opening the padlock.

At the back of the shed he picks the two soundest planks he can find. He checks each for rot with a thumbnail and a knock before Bram takes one. He grabs a short length of cord or spare rope from the racks for lashing as well.

"Quick as we can," he says to the others, squinting at the sun. "Gate shut, keys back in his hand, and on the road by noon. Thorn's coach won't wait for heroes."

scenes.narration:
Pell wrings the worst of the water out of his sleeves onto the planking and pats his pouch. The three square keys are still there, cold and wet.

Osric hears him out about the loop. He looks at the hempen line where it comes down over the far lip and into the black water. It's tied twice round the beam that's lying in the hole, out of his reach.

"Rope's on the beam. Beam's down there." He shifts onto his belly beside the sluice-frame and gets one fist round an iron spoke of the wheel, with his elbow hooked through behind it. "Holding iron. Bolted in rock. Go."

Pell's last remark, about *seep* in the book instead of *drowned*, reaches the warden too. Osric doesn't answer it. He works his jaw once and looks at the wheel.

Pell takes the walk at a quick, careful trot. The planks are dry under the chalk and every tread holds, the same as on the way down. The air thins and warms with each switchback until the sun hits him at the top, and his soaked jerkin starts to steam. His shout about the two planks, lashed side by side across the hole, booms down the walk ahead of him and comes back off the walls. On the block at the head of the walk the sealed case sits where Osric left it, square in the light, with the pack beside it. He tosses a crooked grin back down the walk over his shoulder and heads across the yard.

The tool-shed padlock is the same honest country iron as before, and it opens with a turn of the key. Inside it's dim and smells of oil and dry ash-wood: racks of wedges and feathers, spare hafts stacked like kindling. On the inside of the door, at the height of a man's eyes, somebody has drawn a mule in chalk. It's lopsided, its ears are too long, and a sack is slung over its back. Underneath, in big leaning capitals, someone has written PAY THE MULE. Someone else has added a second, smaller *ALSO US* below it.

The planks are at the back, stacked on two trestles to keep them off the floor. There are six of them, twelve-foot walk-planks as thick as a man's hand is wide and grey with age. Pell works down the stack with his thumbnail and his knuckles. The top one rings sound. The second has a split running a third of its length from one end, so he leaves it. The third and fourth are both good, hard to the thumbnail all along and solid under a knock from end to end. He hauls the two good ones off the trestles one at a time. They're heavy enough that he takes each by one end and walks it round. Both end up leaning by the door with their ends in the sunlight. From a nail by the haft-rack he takes a hank of tarred cord, the stuff the crew used to bind haft-heads, and slings it over his shoulder.

Outside, the sun stands well up over the eastern rim of the quarry. It's still a long way short of noon, and white dust drifts across the empty yard. Down at the far end the cool air still rises out of the lower cut.

 (Out of game:)
1) Pell didn't put the loop on himself. He asked Osric to put it on, and Osric said no aloud, giving his reason: the rope is tied round the beam down in the hole, where he can't reach it.
2) Pell's walk up the sound planks and across the yard needs no roll, because that ground has already held everyone's weight.
3) Picking out sound planks with a thumbnail and a knock, and taking cord off a nail, is ordinary handling, so there's no roll.
4) Pell opened the padlock with its own key, so there was nothing uncertain to roll for.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, get yourself up into the fresh air. I’ll fetch the planks—need that key.”

Once I have it, I go to the tool-shed and fetch two sound twelve-foot walk-planks, checking them for rot or splits before carrying them down.

“Osric, show us where they can bear on solid rock your side. No rotten lip taking the load.”

With his guidance, I slide the planks across from the sound walkway, keeping my weight back until both ends have firm support. I mean to make a stable bridge, not another trap.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets go of the silk only when Pell's hands close on the plank and he has his breath. She doesn't fuss. One look, one steadying nod, and she tucks the glowing stone under her arm so both hands are free.

"I don't need a temple's leave to thank mine," she says. "The Lantern sent the light; I only aimed it." She kneels, sets her back against the rail, and begins to move along the floor of the walk toward the tool-shed end of things, using the hempen line to keep anything loose from trailing into the gap. "If you're standing, Pell, you can hold the light and watch the rope. We still need to get Osric off that rock."

She lifts her head and calls to the warden. "Spare walk-planks, back of the tool-shed. We'll bring them to the head of your side. Can you take them with a rope, or does one of us step out with an end?" She doesn't offer to make that crossing; her weight won't serve where rotten stone gives way.

Then she looks to Bram and Pell. "Two planks, laid clean across to sound rock. Fix them at both ends before a boot touches the middle. We don't lift him across empty air and hope the boards are honest when they've sat by a shed all winter."

She starts toward the yard, sure-footed, the light bobbing against her side. She calls back once: "And Pell? Drink's owed from Maela's coin. Let's be quick — the case won't carry itself."Pell reaches into his dripping vest and passes Bram two stones. He says they'll hold the lash we daren't trust; to beat them into the joists beside the planks if the boards move wrong; and that a pin that catches beats a fall that kills. Then he turns to you. His face is still wet, but his voice has steadied. He says the light was yours, and he's glad it landed where it did. He says you didn't just aim it, you counted the count it came in on. He'll stand the watch now, take Frost from his pack, and watch the water; with the rope hand-tended, the sound will tell them if the weight leaves it.

Then he stops above the hole and his face darkens. He says Osric never tied himself to the frame, and he was the one who said nobody goes below without a line. He wants to put his line around Osric before the planks go over, in case the wheel turns and the gate takes him.

He asks if you and Bram can haul cross-wise if Osric slips, once he has a line on, and says no rope will save him if the foul air lies thick in the low cut.

Bram assures Pell he and you will set posts to straddle the crossing, and that any plank that is poor will be good only for fire. He tells Pell to hold the cut and watch for his whistle. Then he asks you whether it's safer to drop a weighted line or a manned line; he means to get the boards across to Osric by cords, rather than trusting the reach.

You take in Pell's words and Bram's, and make your own call. You tell Pell he has the watch, to keep the light, and to lay a line on Osric before any plank goes over. You tell Bram planks by cords, not by arms, and two planks, pinned at both ends before a boot touches them.

The planks wait at the back of the tool-shed, flat in a patch of starry chickweed under the eastern wall. There are four, lifted clear of the soil on bricks to keep the ground from them. Twelve-foot timbers, two fingers thick, cross-braced with iron bars let into their underfaces and spiked at the butt ends. Two are sound. A third has a black-rimmed hole halfway down, as if a nail had worked loose and let water in. The fourth is cracked from a side margin, across the grain a full hand's width. The patch of shade doesn't mask it. The floor of the shed trembles when Bram walks for the planks. It rights itself when he doesn't.

Bram says the two with the iron bars are the ones to carry. With his knife he taps the cracked one and the holed one and sets them aside, then drags the first good board out into the sun. Pell runs his eye along the pair of them and asks whether the cut face of the hole is enough. Osric's voice comes back from the shaft: "No need to cross. Two ropes on a loop. Push the boards over on a fart of a bridge. Wheel first." Pell answers the warden that the wheel is still his to turn, and that you'll be quick, and asks you for the line over the void. He says let it carry axes, not men.

You drew the group around the task with the planks: Pell and Bram carry them by cords; you send the line over by cords first, axes and pins, then the boards, then fix them hard at both ends before any boot goes on them; the wheel is the first work.

Thus ends Round 14. +

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes one look at the chalk mule and snorts. *PAY THE MULE. ALSO US.* He taps the drawing with a knuckle on his way past, the way you'd touch a shrine for luck.

"Bram!" he calls across the yard. "Planks are out, two good ones. Take one, I'll drag the other." He snaps the padlock shut on the tool-shed, tugs it once, and gets his shoulder under the end of the second plank. He's no ox, so he walks it more than carries it, one end bumping in the dust behind him.

At the head of the walk he stops for one breath by the pack and the case and checks both by eye: case sealed, cord and wax as they were. Then he starts down with the plank, careful on the switchbacks, calling ahead before he's in sight:

"Coming down, Warden! Two planks, cord for lashing. Hold your iron."

On the last sound plank he crouches and sets to work quickly. He lays the first plank's end on the sound planking, then pushes it out across the hole by inches until the far end grounds on Osric's bolted rock. He feels for it to sit flat and not rock, and calls "Warden, tell me when it's on solid stone, not rim." Then the second goes alongside it. He lashes the near ends together with the tarred cord, and lashes them both to the rail-post or the end of the sound planking, whatever's spiked in, with tight turns and a knot that won't slip when wet.

Before he steps out, he unties his silk line from the post, makes a fresh loop round his own chest, and hands the free end up to Bram. "Hold it in your hands this time, not on a post." He passes the second hank-end of tarred cord, or the coil's slack, out across the bridge to Osric. "And you, tie on to something before I come over."

Then he crosses: low, feet square, one at a time, weight in the middle of the two boards, eyes on the far end and not the water. On the rock he plants himself beside Osric at the wheel and sets both hands on the rusted spokes.

"Two men, two hands each, like you said." A crooked grin through the drying chalk on his face. "Your count this time."

screens.Pell Dunmore:
Bram came down the walk testing the treads and knocking his shield on the rail at the turns. By the time he reached the yard the tool-shed door already stood open, and two grey planks leaned beside it. He ran a thumbnail along each and knocked on them, found both sound and ringing, and shouldered the first as if he'd carried timber all his life.

You tapped the chalk mule on your way out, snapped the padlock shut, tugged it once, and walked the second plank across the yard with its back end scraping white furrows in the dust.

Sefa had already gone up the cut with the glowing stone under one arm, keeping the hempen line along the foot of the rail so no loop could catch a boot. Halfway up she called down to the warden, asking whether he could take the planks on a rope or whether someone had to step out with an end. Osric answered, short and flat, that you should push them over and he would take the ends.

At the second switchback she stepped into the angle of the rail to let you and Bram pass with the timber. As you went by she told you quietly that the Lantern had sent the light and she had only aimed it, and that your drink could come out of Maela's coin if you were quick about it. Then she went on up into the sun. At the head of the walk the sealed case and your pack sat side by side on the block. You spared them one look: the cord was still crossed and the grey wax unbroken.

You called down a warning to the warden, slipped your silk line off the first rail-post and coiled it as you went. You and Bram set the planks down on the last sound tread with a double thump.

Bram asked Osric where they would bear. The warden laid his whole palm flat on the rock beside the foot of the sluice-frame, a long stride back from the crumbling rim. "Here. Where the bolts go in. Not the edge. Edge is rot under chalk."

Bram slid the first plank out across the hole, kneeling on the butt end with his weight back and feeding it out a forearm at a time while you steadied it from the side. It crossed eight feet of open air above the black water, passed over the broken rim without touching it, and grounded where Osric's hand lay. Osric thumped it with the side of his fist and rocked it. It didn't move. "Rock."

The second plank went over beside it the same way, and Osric thumped that one too. You bound the two near ends together with tarred cord, then to the nearest rail-post with a knot that only tightens when wet, and tossed the rest of the hank across to Osric, telling him to tie on before you came over.

He caught it and lashed the two far ends to the foot of the sluice-frame, below the bolt-heads, hauling each turn down hard. Only then did he pass the cord once round his own middle and once round an iron bolt-head, and knot it. "Boards. Then me."

You made a fresh loop of silk under your arms and held the coil out to Bram, free end on top, telling him to hold it in his hands this time, not on a post. You set the coil against his knee, where he still knelt on the butts of the planks.

Then you crossed, low, each foot square in the middle of the two boards, eyes on the far end and never on the water. The planks gave a little but didn't twist, and nothing creaked that shouldn't. Four steps and you stood on the bolted rock beside Osric, close enough to smell rust and chalk and the wet rag over his beard. You put both hands on the rusted spokes and said it was two men, two hands each, and his count this time.

Osric set his hands on the spokes across from yours and breathed in through the rag. "One. Two. *Three.*"

You both threw your weight into it together.

scenes.input:
(Round 14 — one paragraph per character in this scene. Close this scene on the world as it stands: no question, offer, demand or wait put to one character, and no out-of-game note — the table asks every player what they do next.)

Bram Halloway: “Pell, get yourself up into the fresh air. I’ll fetch the planks—need that key.”

Once I have it, I go to the tool-shed and fetch two sound twelve-foot walk-planks, checking them for rot or splits before carrying them down.

“Osric, show us where they can bear on solid rock your side. No rotten lip taking the load.”

With his guidance, I slide the planks across from the sound walkway, keeping my weight back until both ends have firm support. I mean to make a stable bridge, not another trap.

Sefa Marrin: Sefa lets go of the silk only when Pell's hands close on the plank and he has his breath. She doesn't fuss. One look, one steadying nod, and she tucks the glowing stone under her arm so both hands are free.

"I don't need a temple's leave to thank mine," she says. "The Lantern sent the light; I only aimed it." She kneels, sets her back against the rail, and begins to move along the floor of the walk toward the tool-shed end of things, using the hempen line to keep anything loose from trailing into the gap. "If you're standing, Pell, you can hold the light and watch the rope. We still need to get Osric off that rock."

She lifts her head and calls to the warden. "Spare walk-planks, back of the tool-shed. We'll bring them to the head of your side. Can you take them with a rope, or does one of us step out with an end?" She doesn't offer to make that crossing; her weight won't serve where rotten stone gives way.

Then she looks to Bram and Pell. "Two planks, laid clean across to sound rock. Fix them at both ends before a boot touches the middle. We don't lift him across empty air and hope the boards are honest when they've sat by a shed all winter."

She starts toward the yard, sure-footed, the light bobbing against her side. She calls back once: "And Pell? Drink's owed from Maela's coin. Let's be quick — the case won't carry itself."Pell reaches into his dripping vest and passes Bram two stones. He says they'll hold the lash we daren't trust; to beat them into the joists beside the planks if the boards move wrong; and that a pin that catches beats a fall that kills. Then he turns to you. His face is still wet, but his voice has steadied. He says the light was yours, and he's glad it landed where it did. He says you didn't just aim it, you counted the count it came in on. He'll stand the watch now, take Frost from his pack, and watch the water; with the rope hand-tended, the sound will tell them if the weight leaves it.

Then he stops above the hole and his face darkens. He says Osric never tied himself to the frame, and he was the one who said nobody goes below without a line. He wants to put his line around Osric before the planks go over, in case the wheel turns and the gate takes him.

He asks if you and Bram can haul cross-wise if Osric slips, once he has a line on, and says no rope will save him if the foul air lies thick in the low cut.

Bram assures Pell he and you will set posts to straddle the crossing, and that any plank that is poor will be good only for fire. He tells Pell to hold the cut and watch for his whistle. Then he asks you whether it's safer to drop a weighted line or a manned line; he means to get the boards across to Osric by cords, rather than trusting the reach.

You take in Pell's words and Bram's, and make your own call. You tell Pell he has the watch, to keep the light, and to lay a line on Osric before any plank goes over. You tell Bram planks by cords, not by arms, and two planks, pinned at both ends before a boot touches them.

The planks wait at the back of the tool-shed, flat in a patch of starry chickweed under the eastern wall. There are four, lifted clear of the soil on bricks to keep the ground from them. Twelve-foot timbers, two fingers thick, cross-braced with iron bars let into their underfaces and spiked at the butt ends. Two are sound. A third has a black-rimmed hole halfway down, as if a nail had worked loose and let water in. The fourth is cracked from a side margin, across the grain a full hand's width. The patch of shade doesn't mask it. The floor of the shed trembles when Bram walks for the planks. It rights itself when he doesn't.

Bram says the two with the iron bars are the ones to carry. With his knife he taps the cracked one and the holed one and sets them aside, then drags the first good board out into the sun. Pell runs his eye along the pair of them and asks whether the cut face of the hole is enough. Osric's voice comes back from the shaft: "No need to cross. Two ropes on a loop. Push the boards over on a fart of a bridge. Wheel first." Pell answers the warden that the wheel is still his to turn, and that you'll be quick, and asks you for the line over the void. He says let it carry axes, not men.

You drew the group around the task with the planks: Pell and Bram carry them by cords; you send the line over by cords first, axes and pins, then the boards, then fix them hard at both ends before any boot goes on them; the wheel is the first work.

Thus ends Round 14. +

Where you are: tool-shed side of the yard, with the planks in the sun · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 15 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell Dunmore: Pell takes one look at the chalk mule and snorts. *PAY THE MULE. ALSO US.* He taps the drawing with a knuckle on his way past, the way you'd touch a shrine for luck.

"Bram!" he calls across the yard. "Planks are out, two good ones. Take one, I'll drag the other." He snaps the padlock shut on the tool-shed, tugs it once, and gets his shoulder under the end of the second plank. He's no ox, so he walks it more than carries it, one end bumping in the dust behind him.

At the head of the walk he stops for one breath by the pack and the case and checks both by eye: case sealed, cord and wax as they were. Then he starts down with the plank, careful on the switchbacks, calling ahead before he's in sight:

"Coming down, Warden! Two planks, cord for lashing. Hold your iron."

On the last sound plank he crouches and sets to work quickly. He lays the first plank's end on the sound planking, then pushes it out across the hole by inches until the far end grounds on Osric's bolted rock. He feels for it to sit flat and not rock, and calls "Warden, tell me when it's on solid stone, not rim." Then the second goes alongside it. He lashes the near ends together with the tarred cord, and lashes them both to the rail-post or the end of the sound planking, whatever's spiked in, with tight turns and a knot that won't slip when wet.

Before he steps out, he unties his silk line from the post, makes a fresh loop round his own chest, and hands the free end up to Bram. "Hold it in your hands this time, not on a post." He passes the second hank-end of tarred cord, or the coil's slack, out across the bridge to Osric. "And you, tie on to something before I come over."

Then he crosses: low, feet square, one at a time, weight in the middle of the two boards, eyes on the far end and not the water. On the rock he plants himself beside Osric at the wheel and sets both hands on the rusted spokes.

"Two men, two hands each, like you said." A crooked grin through the drying chalk on his face. "Your count this time."

On the third pull the old screw took and kept turning, the iron groaning in its threads. Under the frame a wooden gate as thick as a door slid down its grooves, pushing a fold of black water ahead of it. It seated with a deep, solid knock that came back off every wall of the cut, and stopped.

The water beyond the sluice stopped sucking at the boards. Somewhere under the ledge the gurgle in the drain went quiet.

Osric let go of the spokes and looked at his palms, red to the wrist, then at Pell's, just as red. "Two men." He breathed out through the rag. "Hasn't turned that sweet since I had hair."

He worked the cord loose from the bolt-head and from round his middle and coiled it over his forearm without hurrying. The lashed planks lie across the hole between the rock and the walk. Pell's silk runs from his chest back over them to the coil at your knee. Down in the flooded working, through the gap beside the boards, the cork still turns by the far wall. Up at the head of the cut Sefa stands in the full sun beside the sealed case and the pack, the white stone faint under her arm in the daylight. It's well short of noon. The lower cutting-shed still stands unlocked at the top of the slope.

relay.request:
Characters at the table: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
In this scene: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.
Write the screens of, in this order: Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin, Pell Dunmore.

What the players wrote for this round, in the round's order (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Bram Halloway: “Pell, get yourself up into the fresh air. I’ll fetch the planks—need that key.”

Once I have it, I go to the tool-shed and fetch two sound twelve-foot walk-planks, checking them for rot or splits before carrying them down.

“Osric, show us where they can bear on solid rock your side. No rotten lip taking the load.”

With his guidance, I slide the planks across from the sound walkway, keeping my weight back until both ends have firm support. I mean to make a stable bridge, not another trap.

Sefa Marrin: Sefa lets go of the silk only when Pell's hands close on the plank and he has his breath. She doesn't fuss. One look, one steadying nod, and she tucks the glowing stone under her arm so both hands are free.

"I don't need a temple's leave to thank mine," she says. "The Lantern sent the light; I only aimed it." She kneels, sets her back against the rail, and begins to move along the floor of the walk toward the tool-shed end of things, using the hempen line to keep anything loose from trailing into the gap. "If you're standing, Pell, you can hold the light and watch the rope. We still need to get Osric off that rock."

She lifts her head and calls to the warden. "Spare walk-planks, back of the tool-shed. We'll bring them to the head of your side. Can you take them with a rope, or does one of us step out with an end?" She doesn't offer to make that crossing; her weight won't serve where rotten stone gives way.

Then she looks to Bram and Pell. "Two planks, laid clean across to sound rock. Fix them at both ends before a boot touches the middle. We don't lift him across empty air and hope the boards are honest when they've sat by a shed all winter."

She starts toward the yard, sure-footed, the light bobbing against her side. She calls back once: "And Pell? Drink's owed from Maela's coin. Let's be quick — the case won't carry itself."Pell reaches into his dripping vest and passes Bram two stones. He says they'll hold the lash we daren't trust; to beat them into the joists beside the planks if the boards move wrong; and that a pin that catches beats a fall that kills. Then he turns to you. His face is still wet, but his voice has steadied. He says the light was yours, and he's glad it landed where it did. He says you didn't just aim it, you counted the count it came in on. He'll stand the watch now, take Frost from his pack, and watch the water; with the rope hand-tended, the sound will tell them if the weight leaves it.

Then he stops above the hole and his face darkens. He says Osric never tied himself to the frame, and he was the one who said nobody goes below without a line. He wants to put his line around Osric before the planks go over, in case the wheel turns and the gate takes him.

He asks if you and Bram can haul cross-wise if Osric slips, once he has a line on, and says no rope will save him if the foul air lies thick in the low cut.

Bram assures Pell he and you will set posts to straddle the crossing, and that any plank that is poor will be good only for fire. He tells Pell to hold the cut and watch for his whistle. Then he asks you whether it's safer to drop a weighted line or a manned line; he means to get the boards across to Osric by cords, rather than trusting the reach.

You take in Pell's words and Bram's, and make your own call. You tell Pell he has the watch, to keep the light, and to lay a line on Osric before any plank goes over. You tell Bram planks by cords, not by arms, and two planks, pinned at both ends before a boot touches them.

The planks wait at the back of the tool-shed, flat in a patch of starry chickweed under the eastern wall. There are four, lifted clear of the soil on bricks to keep the ground from them. Twelve-foot timbers, two fingers thick, cross-braced with iron bars let into their underfaces and spiked at the butt ends. Two are sound. A third has a black-rimmed hole halfway down, as if a nail had worked loose and let water in. The fourth is cracked from a side margin, across the grain a full hand's width. The patch of shade doesn't mask it. The floor of the shed trembles when Bram walks for the planks. It rights itself when he doesn't.

Bram says the two with the iron bars are the ones to carry. With his knife he taps the cracked one and the holed one and sets them aside, then drags the first good board out into the sun. Pell runs his eye along the pair of them and asks whether the cut face of the hole is enough. Osric's voice comes back from the shaft: "No need to cross. Two ropes on a loop. Push the boards over on a fart of a bridge. Wheel first." Pell answers the warden that the wheel is still his to turn, and that you'll be quick, and asks you for the line over the void. He says let it carry axes, not men.

You drew the group around the task with the planks: Pell and Bram carry them by cords; you send the line over by cords first, axes and pins, then the boards, then fix them hard at both ends before any boot goes on them; the wheel is the first work.

Thus ends Round 14. +

Where you are: tool-shed side of the yard, with the planks in the sun · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 15 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell Dunmore: Pell takes one look at the chalk mule and snorts. *PAY THE MULE. ALSO US.* He taps the drawing with a knuckle on his way past, the way you'd touch a shrine for luck.

"Bram!" he calls across the yard. "Planks are out, two good ones. Take one, I'll drag the other." He snaps the padlock shut on the tool-shed, tugs it once, and gets his shoulder under the end of the second plank. He's no ox, so he walks it more than carries it, one end bumping in the dust behind him.

At the head of the walk he stops for one breath by the pack and the case and checks both by eye: case sealed, cord and wax as they were. Then he starts down with the plank, careful on the switchbacks, calling ahead before he's in sight:

"Coming down, Warden! Two planks, cord for lashing. Hold your iron."

On the last sound plank he crouches and sets to work quickly. He lays the first plank's end on the sound planking, then pushes it out across the hole by inches until the far end grounds on Osric's bolted rock. He feels for it to sit flat and not rock, and calls "Warden, tell me when it's on solid stone, not rim." Then the second goes alongside it. He lashes the near ends together with the tarred cord, and lashes them both to the rail-post or the end of the sound planking, whatever's spiked in, with tight turns and a knot that won't slip when wet.

Before he steps out, he unties his silk line from the post, makes a fresh loop round his own chest, and hands the free end up to Bram. "Hold it in your hands this time, not on a post." He passes the second hank-end of tarred cord, or the coil's slack, out across the bridge to Osric. "And you, tie on to something before I come over."

Then he crosses: low, feet square, one at a time, weight in the middle of the two boards, eyes on the far end and not the water. On the rock he plants himself beside Osric at the wheel and sets both hands on the rusted spokes.

"Two men, two hands each, like you said." A crooked grin through the drying chalk on his face. "Your count this time."

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I take Pell’s silk line firmly in both hands and brace on the sound walkway.

“Job done. Come across one at a time, low and steady. Pell first, while he’s on the line. Then we’ll send the loop back for you, Osric.”

I take in slack as Pell crosses, without pulling him off balance. Once he’s safe, I pass the loop back for Osric and tend his crossing the same way.

“Then fresh air, lock that last shed, collect your tally-book, and we’re off. Nobody else goes down here today.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell looks at his red palms, then at Osric's, and laughs once, short and surprised. "Rust knew it was outnumbered."

He's already working the silk loop off over his head. He holds it out to the warden. "You first. You've got no line, and I've had my swim for the day. Bram's holding the other end, in his hands this time." He waits until Osric has the loop under his arms, then calls up the walk: "Bram! Warden's coming over on my silk. Take him in like a bale."

Once Osric is on the planks, Pell crosses after him the way he came: low, feet square in the middle of the boards, four steps. He glances once down the gap at the cork turning by the far wall and the carved block lying face to the plaster.

"Planks stay or go, Warden? Your yard." Whichever Osric says, he does it.

On the way up he stops at the low cutting-shed. He doesn't step inside. He pulls the swollen door shut, snaps the last padlock and tugs it once. Then he takes a stub of chalk from the bench by the door, or from his own pocket, and writes across the planks at eye height in big leaning capitals, like the mule's: FLOOR ROTTEN. NO FIRE. Under it, smaller: *SEE OSRIC.*

At the top he drops the three square keys into Osric's palm, one at a time so the man can count them. "Back in your hand before we walk, like you said." He shoulders his pack, checks the side pocket by feel, and glances at the case without touching it.

"When you're in Beregost asking Thorn your question, ask at the Song of the Morning too." He tips his head back toward the cut. "Sun cut in stone, plaster that drinks light. Lathander's lot left it. They might pay to have it back, which is more than Vandarren's done lately."

He squints at the sun, still short of noon, and starts down the cart track toward Beregost, dripping white dust off his boots.

"Come on. Thorn's coach, Teague's ledger, eleven men's wages. Long walk, and I'm wet."

Bram Halloway: I take Pell’s silk line firmly in both hands and brace on the sound walkway.

“Job done. Come across one at a time, low and steady. Pell first, while he’s on the line. Then we’ll send the loop back for you, Osric.”

I take in slack as Pell crosses, without pulling him off balance. Once he’s safe, I pass the loop back for Osric and tend his crossing the same way.

“Then fresh air, lock that last shed, collect your tally-book, and we’re off. Nobody else goes down here today.”

Pell Dunmore: Pell looks at his red palms, then at Osric's, and laughs once, short and surprised. "Rust knew it was outnumbered."

He's already working the silk loop off over his head. He holds it out to the warden. "You first. You've got no line, and I've had my swim for the day. Bram's holding the other end, in his hands this time." He waits until Osric has the loop under his arms, then calls up the walk: "Bram! Warden's coming over on my silk. Take him in like a bale."

Once Osric is on the planks, Pell crosses after him the way he came: low, feet square in the middle of the boards, four steps. He glances once down the gap at the cork turning by the far wall and the carved block lying face to the plaster.

"Planks stay or go, Warden? Your yard." Whichever Osric says, he does it.

On the way up he stops at the low cutting-shed. He doesn't step inside. He pulls the swollen door shut, snaps the last padlock and tugs it once. Then he takes a stub of chalk from the bench by the door, or from his own pocket, and writes across the planks at eye height in big leaning capitals, like the mule's: FLOOR ROTTEN. NO FIRE. Under it, smaller: *SEE OSRIC.*

At the top he drops the three square keys into Osric's palm, one at a time so the man can count them. "Back in your hand before we walk, like you said." He shoulders his pack, checks the side pocket by feel, and glances at the case without touching it.

"When you're in Beregost asking Thorn your question, ask at the Song of the Morning too." He tips his head back toward the cut. "Sun cut in stone, plaster that drinks light. Lathander's lot left it. They might pay to have it back, which is more than Vandarren's done lately."

He squints at the sun, still short of noon, and starts down the cart track toward Beregost, dripping white dust off his boots.

"Come on. Thorn's coach, Teague's ledger, eleven men's wages. Long walk, and I'm wet."
