private.text:
Sefa leans out further over the lip of the shaft, so that her voice carries down into the dark as well as across it. She calls to Pell, telling him to answer her and say the word, and says nobody lifts until she hears him speak, not merely a tug on the rope. Then she starts a low, even chant that follows the beat of the counting coming up from the water: stay with the light, over and over, in the cadence of a nurse timing compressions. The hand holding the stone does not waver. Her eyes move along the edge of the black water, searching for where the counting comes from.

Pell's voice reaches the top of the shaft before you have finished bracing. It is hoarse and slow: the flask is in his hand and the cork is out. Then he says something about the silk line and a post that can't haul. Osric's bellow follows, rougher and shorter: Pell has it, and the count should begin. Under the shouting, the low counting from the water starts again.

You don't wait on anyone else's count. You hold the rope, and Osric settled that a lift goes on the voice of whoever holds it. You call down the shaft to Pell, set your heels and count.

"One. Two. Three."

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Sefa Marrin — Human, warlock 5 (The Celestial — the Lantern; Pact of the Tome), former hospice novice, level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 14 · Speed 30 feet
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 18
Skills: Persuasion +7; Arcana +4; Religion +4; Insight +3
Saves: Wisdom saving throw +3 (proficient); Charisma saving throw +7 (proficient); Strength saving throw −1; Dexterity saving throw +2; Constitution saving throw +2; Intelligence saving throw +1
Attacks: Eldritch Blast +7 to hit, two beams, 1d10+4 force each, range 120 feet; Dagger +5 to hit, 1d4+2 piercing, thrown 20/60
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Spell attack +7; spell save DC 15; Pact Magic: two 3rd-level pact slots, recovered only on a short or long rest; Healing Light: a pool of six d6 per long rest; a bonus action spends up to four dice to heal a creature within 60 feet; Pact of the Tome: the Book of Shadows holds three extra cantrips (Guidance, Spare the Dying, Thaumaturgy); Agonizing Blast: +4 to each Eldritch Blast beam's damage; Repelling Blast: a beam that hits pushes the target up to 10 feet away; Eyes of the Rune Keeper: reads all writing
Spells: Eldritch Blast (cantrip); Light (cantrip); Sacred Flame (cantrip); Mage Hand (cantrip); Minor Illusion (cantrip); Guidance (cantrip); Spare the Dying (cantrip); Thaumaturgy (cantrip); Cure Wounds (1); Guiding Bolt (1); Misty Step (2); Lesser Restoration (2); Hold Person (2); Daylight (3)
Limits: Two pact slots only, back only after a rest; Light armour; Strength 8 — weak up close; One concentration spell at a time
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Pact slots 2/2; Healing light 6/6; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 1 pp; 8 gp; 41 sp; 12 cp
Worn: Amulet: Prayer Beads; Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Book of Shadows; Main hand: Dagger
Pack: Bedroll and Rations; Candle ×2; Tinderbox

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell slows to a half-step behind you and Bram, studying the cart, the tools, the sheds and the house. He murmurs to you both that a quarry this quiet and a warden who won't wave means either the crew is on holiday or someone is waiting behind the door, and that you shouldn't all walk up in a bunch. Then he calls out a friendly greeting with an empty hand raised, says Maela Thorn sent you from Beregost for the case, and asks whether the man is the warden. He stays well back from the doorway, leaving open ground between himself and it. Bram sheathes his sword and walks into the yard with his shield at his side, looking over the sheds and ledges. He stops a few paces short of the doorway, asks about the sealed case of dye-salts and whether the man is the warden, and remarks that it is quiet for a working day.

The yard tells most of its story before anyone reaches the door. The dust holds yesterday's tracks: a crowd of hobnailed boots heading down the cart track towards Beregost, side by side and in no hurry. They spread out where men walked abreast, and in one place a dozen stand in a loose ring where somebody stopped to talk. Through the middle runs one line of hoof-prints beside a man's boots, a mule being led rather than driven. There are no drag marks, no scuffs where someone dug in his heels, and nothing has been knocked over. Up close, the tools by the lower cut have not been dropped in a panic. The wedges sit in a neat row on a ledge. One sledgehammer stands upright on its head with the haft pointing at the sky, the way a man leaves a thing he wants people to notice.

There is nobody on the terraces and nobody at the lifting frame. Every shed door is shut and every shutter closed, except the house's single front window, which stands open for the smoke and shows a table, a kettle and nothing else. In the yard you see that one set of fresh tracks goes in and out of the house door and around to the woodpile behind it, and they all belong to the man in the apron.

He doesn't glance back into the house once. He watches your hands, Pell's empty one first, then Bram's on the sword hilt, then yours well clear of your belt. His stance isn't fear. It's the heavy, set-jawed stillness of a man who has been angry for a long time and is tired of it.

He waits until all three of you have asked him the same thing.

"Warden. Osric Hale." He takes a breath through his nose. "Three of you asking. Yes."

To Bram's remark he gives a short look across the empty yard, as though the answer were out there for anyone to see. "Crew walked. Noon bell, yesterday. Left the tools where they stood." He jerks his chin at the upright sledgehammer. "Tools are the house's. So they left them for the house."

He hasn't unfolded his arms. "The case. Thorn's case. It's inside, and it's sealed. I sealed it myself." He pauses. "Thorn paid for it. Paid somebody. Not me. Not a copper to this yard in three weeks, and eleven men's wages owing." He looks at each of you in turn, without heat, the way a man weighs stone. "Vandarren owns this pit. Vandarren's man in the Gate takes the money. So the case stays on my table till somebody tells me where her money went, and when my lads see theirs."

Then he steps back out of the doorway into the dim room and leaves the door open behind him. Inside, a small iron-bound box sits on the table beside the kettle, its lid crossed with cord and a blob of grey wax. Osric drops onto the bench next to it, sets one broad, dust-white hand flat on the lid, and stays there.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: quarry yard, just short of the warden's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You stop just short of the doorstep with your hands open at your sides, and you do not cross into the house. You tell the warden he has every right to be angry, and point at the upright sledgehammer. You say Maela Thorn is not his enemy, and offer to carry the case back before sunset and put his grievance before her. Or he can name whoever in the Gate takes Vandarren's money and say what proof he would need. You ask plainly what it would take, right now, for him to let the box go back to Beregost with you.

Before that, Bram kept his hand off his sword hilt and stayed outside the threshold. He told the warden that eleven men owed three weeks' wages have reason for anger, but that you are hired carriers, not Vandarren's collectors. He said the man in the Gate loses nothing if you return empty-handed, while the warden's lads stay unpaid and so do you. He asked how much is owed in all and whether the warden has any word from Vandarren's agent, a letter, a receipt or a name, to put before Thorn while there is still time.

Pell leans on the window frame, arms on the sill. He speaks of his da and a harbour-wall hammer, then urges Osric to come along to Beregost, carry the case himself with his hand on it, and put the question to Thorn in person: whom did she pay, and when? He asks for Vandarren's man's name and says he knows some doors in the Gate.

Osric hears all three of you out without moving, his hand flat on the lid. Only his eyes move, from Bram at the door to you at the step to Pell at the window, and they rest longest on Pell.

He breathes in through his nose and answers Bram first, because Bram asked for numbers.

"Sixty-one gold. Four silver. Eleven men, eighteen working days, cutters at cutters' rate." He nods at a shelf behind him, where a fat grey canvas ledger sits between a lamp and a crock of nails. "Tally-book has it to the copper." Then, to the rest of what Bram asked: "Name's Aubrin Teague. Vandarren's steward in the Gate. Counting-room off Windspell Street." He reaches under the lid of the bench, pulls out a folded, softened letter and flattens it on the table by the box. "His last. Five weeks back. *Wages to follow with the next cart.*" A short pause. "Cart came. Took salt. Brought nothing."

His eyes move to you. He listens to the whole of what you say without interrupting, and he neither softens nor hardens.

"Didn't say Thorn's my enemy. Said she paid somebody. You say Vandarren's man. Maybe. Haven't seen it." He taps the letter once. "Your word's a good word, likely. Still yours. Not hers. Not Teague's."

Then he turns to the window and keeps his eyes on Pell a long moment.

"My own hand on it. Ask her to her face." Something in the set of his mouth eases, not into a smile. "That I'd do."

He gets up heavily, his hand still on the case, and looks out past Pell at the yard: the cart, the frame, the row of sheds with shut doors, the dark mouth of the lower cut beyond.

"Can't walk off and leave her standing open, though." You understand he means the quarry. "Thirty years. Sheds locked. Frame pinned, ropes in. Mule-shed's empty, no matter. Sluice-gate in the low cut wants shutting, or the seep backs up the drain by morning." His eyes stay on the lower cut a little longer than on the rest. "Hour's work. Less, with hands."

He folds Teague's letter once and puts it inside his apron. Then he lifts the iron-bound box and tucks it under one arm as easily as a loaf, and takes the ring of keys from his belt. He comes out past Bram into the sun, pulls the house door shut and locks it from outside, case still under his arm. He sets off across the yard towards the first shed. Dust puffs white around his boots, and the lower cut waits at the far end of the yard. Its walls are stained darker than the rest of the quarry, and cool air drifts up out of it, smelling of standing water.

Where you are: outside the warden's house in the quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell steps up beside the warden and says an hour's work will be less with more hands. He suggests Bram handle the lifting frame and ropes, and that you take the tally-book and letter to check against what Osric has told you, if Osric allows it. He asks for the keys to the sheds and says he'll go down to the sluice with Osric. He asks whether the gate is stiff or something else is wrong. Bram says he'll help, asks Osric about the footing, loose stone and deep water in the lower cut, and offers to take the heavy work.

Osric hears you out without breaking stride. When you offer to hold a light where the sun won't reach, he gives you a short sideways look, the first that seems to take you for something other than trouble. "Fair." A few steps on, about the cut, he says: "Water. Cold. Air sits heavy low down, so nobody lingers. You do the job and come up." It sounds like a rule he says so often he no longer hears it.

To Bram he gives a longer answer. He stops at the edge of the yard and points out the sheds, the spoil heaps and the ground sloping down to the lower cut. The footing is good on the crew's track, planked where it's wet. The whole hill is old workings, some shored and some forgotten, so keep to the trodden dust. The top terrace has loose stone and nobody is going up there today.

He works three square-headed iron keys off his ring and drops them in Pell's palm. They are for the sheds and must come back to his hand before you walk. The tally-book stays with him, since the house is locked and it goes to Beregost. You can read it on the road, every line. He doesn't take the letter out of his apron. He nods to Pell's offer to see the sluice: "Gate's stiff. Rust. Wants two hands on the wheel." He doesn't answer whether anything else is wrong down there, and he isn't looking at the cut as he leaves it unanswered.

The work goes dusty, simple and faster with more hands. Bram works the windlass and pin on the lifting frame, then walks the boom down onto its trestle. The ropes come in as three long hawsers stiff with chalk. Bram coils them, and you take the end of each as it comes off, walk it out straight so it doesn't kink, and carry the coils to the rope-shed two at a time. It's heavier than you'd like, and your arms tell you so. Pell goes down the row of sheds with the keys.

When the last coil is in, you cross the yard dusting your hands on your skirts. Osric has come down the slope with the box under his arm and stopped at the plank walk into the lower cut. Below, the cut opens downward in stained steps, its walls darker than the rest of the quarry, until a sheet of still black water fills the bottom. At the water's edge stands a wooden sluice-frame with an iron wheel, its spokes red with rust. The cool air keeps rising out of it, steady as breath.

Where you are: quarry yard, by the plank walk into the lower cut · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell stops at the threshold of the low shed and leaves the lock alone. He pulls his collar up over his mouth and breathes shallow, then crouches by the cold brazier without touching it. He takes a pinch of the pink crust, smells it with his arm held out, and wraps it in a twist of rag, then checks the stained boards along the cut-side wall with his knife-tip. Without turning, he says quietly to you that you should come smell the ash but not breathe deep: pink ash and burnt sugar, no stonecutter's fire. He steps out, pulls the door to without locking it, and walks to the plank walk where Osric waits. He holds up the folded rag and asks whether it's the dye-salts, Thorn's goods, or whether someone else had a fire down here, and whether that's why the air below sits so thick. He keeps the third key in his own hand rather than giving it back.

Bram, at the head of the walk, studies the boards and supports of the way down to the wheel. He presses Osric on whether there is any trouble below beyond rust and foul air, since the crew should know before they lay hands on it. He takes out his rope and proposes tying a line to whoever works the wheel, with another person holding it from the top, so a dizzy man can be hauled up and nobody has to go down after him. He asks whether your light can do without a flame.

The walk is sound. The planks are thick and newer than the sheds, spiked into cut stone steps that drop in tiers towards the black water. The crew kept their track in repair. Only the last stretch is bare. At the bottom a broad ledge of wet stone runs along the water to the sluice-frame, dark with seep, and from up here nobody could say what lies under it.

You pick a flat white stone out of the dust and speak a word over it. Light blooms on it, clean and steady, bright enough to throw shadows at noon. You hold it out to Pell, lay two fingers on his wrist and murmur a prayer for steady hands. Something warm and steady settles into his hands under your touch.

Osric looks at the rag Pell holds up, then at Pell. He breathes in through his nose.

"Salt. Thorn's salt." He tips his head towards the cut. "Grows on the walls down there. Pink crust. Lads scrape it in the wet, I case it." He glances at the shed. "Chips get in with the coal. Fire burns sweet. Shed goes sleepy. Told 'em. No salt in the fire." He pauses. "Air's heavy. Always was."

Then Bram asks him straight out, with the rope already in his hands, and the warden looks at the coil for a moment before he answers.

"Lost a man down there. Tobin Reed. Three years back." His voice stays level. "Four feet of water. Found him in it. Face down, like he'd gone to sleep." A short silence. "Drink, I wrote."

"Line's good," Osric says to Bram, and he means it. "Wheel wants two hands on it. Me and one. Line on both. Down, wheel, up. Nobody sits."

He looks at the iron-bound box under his arm, then at the three of you. Then he bends and sets it on a flat block at the head of the walk, square in the sun, where anyone on the walk or at the wheel can see it. He leaves his hand on the lid a moment longer than he needs to. "Stays there."

He straightens up and holds out his hand for the end of Bram's rope. Below, the cool air keeps rising out of the cut, and on the ledge the rusted wheel waits by the still black water.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Lantern-lit Stone
Conditions: Concentrating: Guidance

Where you are: head of the plank walk above the cut · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 5 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram tied a loop for Osric and one around himself, leaving a fathom of slack between them. He told Pell and you to tend the line and keep it out of the water, and said he would go down only if the fifty-foot line reached the ledge with enough left for hauling from safe ground. He walked the free end down the plank walk to check. The walk switches back across the stepped tiers, forty-odd feet of planking from head to ledge. With two men tied a fathom apart at the bottom, the tail of the line would end on the second tier from the top, and nobody could haul from there without standing on the walk. Bram stayed at the top by his own rule. Osric looked at the coil, then at the drop, and grunted. The loop stayed round his chest, and the hempen line now runs from Bram at the head of the walk down to the warden.

Pell told the others that he had sniffed the ash once and nearly yawned his jaw off, and that he doubted Tobin was drunk. He wet a rag over his nose and mouth and gave Osric a wet strip. He asked you to count aloud from the top and keep your light on the men's faces, not the water, so you could see their eyes. He tied a silk line under his arms with a slip-knot and put the free end in Bram's hand. He asked Osric quietly about the floor of the low shed and whether there was an old working under it.

You took your post behind Bram's right shoulder with one foot braced on bare stone. The lit stone in your hand throws its clean light down the first two tiers. When you said *one at a time*, Osric glanced back at you once and didn't argue.

Pell's words about the ash and Tobin landed on Osric and stayed there. He didn't answer. He breathed in through his nose, took the wet rag, and tied it over his beard. Asked about the shed floor, he looked back up the slope at the low shed. "Old working. Shed's built over the mouth of it." He paused. "Knew the boards were soft. On my list. Nobody stands there."

Pell followed Osric down. The walk is sound, and every tread he tested held. At the bottom Osric stepped onto the ledge, walked the ten feet to the sluice-frame, and set both hands on the rusted wheel. Pell came after him, keeping his eyes on the ledge.

Then the ledge opened under Pell. He dropped eight feet through a rush of rotten wood and wet chalk. The silk line snapped taut around Bram's fist as he hit bottom. It hangs straight up through the hole with a man on the end of it, and nobody can lift him while the stone holds. Osric let go of the wheel and went down on his knees on the stone he trusts, at the edge of the hole, with Bram's line tight across his back. He looked down at Pell, then at something below, and for a moment he didn't seem to breathe. "Don't sit," he said, rough. "Keep talking. Keep your head up." Then he shouted up the walk without turning: "Old working under the ledge! Bare stone's bad! Nobody comes on it but by the planks!"

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: Pinned in the Flooded Working

Where you are: head of the plank walk, behind Bram · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 6 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram sets his heels on the bare stone at the head of the walk and takes the strain on both lines without hauling. He tells you to help him hold them and not to step onto the ledge. He calls down to Pell, asking what pins him, whether his head is clear of the water, and whether he can free it if the line takes his weight. He tells Osric to get back onto the planks if it is safe and to put no more weight by the hole. Then he leans on the first rail-post, a stride below him and set in an iron-wedged socket in the rock. It doesn't shift. He takes two turns of the hempen line around it with a half-hitch over them, keeping tension all the while. The post now holds the warden, and Bram has his right hand free and the silk line in his left.

You go down the switchbacks one tread at a time, on planks only. On the last sound plank you stop with one hand on the rail. The broken lip of the hole is an arm's length past the end of the planking. You hold the stone out over the shaft and its light falls straight down. The darkness turns into grey water, a jagged rim of rotten timber, and the tilted white face of a block. Your voice carries across the cut the way it would across a ward at night, and Bram's shout booms off the walls after it.

Osric is on the far side of the hole, the sluice side, with the hole between him and the planks. He looks at it, then presses the heel of his hand on the stone under his knees. "Sluice footing's rock. Frame's bolted in it," he says, not raising his voice, though it reaches the top. The gap is no place to step over, so he will stay on his side. He stretches out flat on his belly with the rope across his back running up to the rail-post, as far from the edge as he can get his weight.

You ask about lowering Pell to a proper floor, and Osric gives you a short look across the hole. "He's on the floor." Then he jerks his head at a black deck-beam lying half-sunk across the corner of the chamber. The beam goes under the block, low edge, rough side, with rope round the far end and up to the lip. Two haul, the beam lifts, and the block tips off him. "Shifted blocks forty years. Comes up easy with the beam. Sits there a week without it."

Your light shows you what he means. The block lies tilted with its carved face up: a sun disc with straight rays and a ring of small cut marks around it. It is the sunburst Lathander's people cut over their doors and on their altar-cloths, cut here into a stone at the bottom of a quarry. The jagged lower edge has gone into the water, and Pell's leg is under it. You have seen this kind of wound on the docks, when a cargo net gave way. The stone has bitten in and is holding the torn flesh shut by its own weight. While the block stays put, the leg won't bleed much. Once it lifts, the wound will open and bleed hard, all at once. Whoever lifts it needs healing ready at that same moment: a potion down his throat, or your light on him.

The wall behind the block, where it once stood, shows a square patch of old grey plaster. Every surface down there is wet: the cut stone, the pink tidemark, the rotten wood. The plaster is the only thing that looks dry. The seep keeps trickling from the crack in the far wall, and the water has risen a hair's breadth against the tidemark.

You hold the stone low over the lip, angled so its light falls on the face below you and leaves the water dark. You talk down to Pell the whole time, unhurried and steady. Bram's half-hitch on the rail-post had already answered your question about an anchor. Osric answered the rest: there is nowhere lower to put a man than the bottom. Your offer of warmth goes down the shaft with your voice and stays offered, and the Lantern's light sits ready in your hands, unspent.

Your records, changed:
Conditions: —

Where you are: on the last sound plank of the walk, above the hole · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 7 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You braced your back against the rail and let the light fall full on Pell's upturned face. Your voice went down the shaft like a bell over water as you gave your order: set the beam, bind the rope round its far end and up over the lip, two to haul, Bram keeping the line, you pouring in four dice of the Lantern's light the instant the weight left the leg, and whoever could reach Pell first kneeling on the wound until you said to ease.

Bram tied the silk line off on the tested rail-post with two turns below the half-hitch on the hempen line, finished with a hitch of his own, and the silk stayed exactly as taut as before. Then he came down the switchbacks plank by plank and stopped on the last sound tread beside you, his shield arm brushing the rail. Before that he had called down to Pell, asking whether Pell could get a rope round the beam without putting his head under it, and telling Pell not to try if he couldn't. He had also asked Osric to tie his line to the sluice-frame instead, so the free end could go to the beam, and to stay tied himself. He said he would stay on the last sound planks and take the hauling end alongside you if the hempen line got round the beam. He asked to be told when it was placed, said they would lift slowly on Osric's word, and asked Pell to say the moment his leg was clear so they could hold it while he moved.

From there you can both see what Osric has done. The hempen line runs from the post above, down along the rail, over the broken lip and into the hole, already tied twice round the old deck-beam. The beam leans up out of the water with its butt against the rotten edge and its tip a foot short of the block's rough lower side. It is set and roped, and the rope Bram was going to ask for is already on it.

Osric lay flat on the sluice side and listened to all you said. When you said *Lantern's light* and *four dice*, he turned his head and looked at the stone glowing in your hand, the way he had looked at the beam, judging what weight it could bear.

He answered Bram first. "Can't." He lifted the hand holding the sluice-wheel just long enough to point at the rope. "That's the lever now. Can't be my line and the beam's too." He gripped the iron spoke again. "Frame's bolted in rock. I hold that." He is still untied.

He looked down at the rope where it crosses the lip, and along its run by the rail, an arm's length from Bram's boots. "You and me haul. You on the rope there, me on the butt from this side. Tip goes under the low edge, the rough one. She tips to the wall." He looked at you. "You don't haul. You do your light."

When you named the sun on the block as Lathander's, Osric did not argue. His eyes went to the square of grey plaster on the wall behind it and stayed there a moment longer than they needed to. He said nothing about it. "Your count, then," he said to you.

Then he looked past you both, up the switchbacks to the head of the walk. Pell's pack lies there on the white stone in the sun, a stride from the sealed case, its side pocket still buckled. Bram came down without it.

"Flask's still up there," he said flatly. "Light's good. I seen your stone." He worked his jaw. "Flask's what I know. Wanted it in my hand before we heave."

He put his free hand on the butt of the beam and left it there, not yet pushing. The seep goes on trickling from the crack in the far wall, and in the grey shaft of light the water stands a little higher against the pink tidemark.

The heave waits on your count.

Where you are: last sound plank of the walk, beside Bram, back to the rail · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 8 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram answers your count before you reach one. He says to hold the lift, that he'll fetch the potion, and he turns and goes back up the switchbacks at a brisk walk. His shield knocks once against the rail at the turn.

You count on regardless, slow and even, and your voice bounces off the stained walls.

"One. Take the strain."

Osric's hand stays flat on the butt of the beam. He doesn't push.

"Two."

The hempen line lies along the rail with nobody on it, still tied off at the post.

"Three. Lift."

Nothing moves. Osric lies on his belly on the bolted rock with his palm on the timber and his other fist round the wheel-spoke. The beam's tip hangs a foot short of the block's rough edge, exactly where he left it. The stone doesn't shift. The light you hold stays behind your ribs, waiting for a moment that hasn't come.

"Not yet," Osric says across the hole, without heat.

Bram's shout carries down the cut from above, saying he is taking a potion from Pell's satchel. After a while he comes back down plank by plank and stops on the last sound tread beside you. He can't reach Osric without crossing the open hole or the rotten skin around it, and he doesn't try. He stands a red flask on the plank at your feet, wedged against the foot of the rail where a stray boot won't send it over. Then he takes the hempen line in both hands along the rail, sets his heels on the sound planking and takes up the slack until the rope tightens. He says he is ready, for a slow lift on your count.

Osric lifts his head and looks at the flask, then down the shaft. He breathes in through the wet rag.

"That's up there." His eyes go to the silk line running taut from the post above, past the rail and down through the hole. "His line's right by you. Flask goes down that. Into his hand. Then three." He settles his palm back on the butt of the beam. "Not before."

Bram's line is tight across the lip. Your light falls steady into the shaft. A drop of seep runs down the wall of the working, reaches the grey plaster and goes around it. In the crack in the far wall the trickle keeps coming, and the water has crept another fingernail's breadth up the pink tidemark.

Where you are: on the last sound plank at the lip of the shaft · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 9 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You tuck the glowing stone into the crook of your arm, bright side out over the hole, and make a small shaping motion over the red flask at your feet. Something takes hold of the flask's neck, little more than a shimmer in the daylight, like heat coming off a summer roof. It lifts the flask clear of the rail-foot and carries it out over the broken lip, then starts down the shaft. The silk line stays as taut as Bram left it, and nothing slides along it or touches it.

Bram keeps both hands on the hempen line, heels set, holding the beam's weight without lifting. Earlier he asked Pell to catch and hold the flask. He told Osric to call a halt if the beam slips, and said you lift only far enough to free Pell's leg, and that he wants a fresh count once Pell has the flask.

Osric turns his head on the bolted rock and watches the flask go down. The red glass catches your light at every hand's breadth of the drop. It passes the jagged rim of rotten timber and the pink ribbons on the walls, then goes into the grey shaft where Pell's free hand is raised out of the water. The shimmer stops a finger's width above his palm and holds the flask there, upright and still.

Osric looks up at Bram. "Slips, I shout." He shifts his palm on the butt of the timber and spreads his fingers. "Can't lift her half. Tip goes under, she tips to the wall or she don't." His eyes go to you. "Your count. When it's his."

Bram's rope creaks once under the strain and goes quiet. The beam's rotten tip hangs a foot short of the block's rough lower edge, dripping into the black water. Down by the far wall the seep keeps trickling through its crack, and the water has crept a little further up the pink tidemark.

Your records, changed:
Conditions: Mage Hand: holds Pell's flask (to ~09:16)

Where you are: at the top of the shaft, by the broken rail, lowering the flask · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 10 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram answers shortly that he understands, and tells Osric to tip the beam to the wall. He keeps his footing and the rope taut with his eyes on the beam. Once Pell has the flask and you have given your count, he means to pull steadily with both hands, working alongside Osric to bring the tip in under the block and roll it over against the wall. He means to keep the strain on until Osric calls the block settled.

You lower the shimmer the last finger's width, and the red flask settles upright into the cup of Pell's raised palm. Glass meets skin. From the last plank you see the glint come to rest on his hand, and a breath later the ripple in the grey light thins out and is gone. The cantrip has run its minute. Nothing holds the flask now except the hand it is sitting in.

Your voice goes down the shaft unhurried: close your fingers, don't drink yet, say when you have it.

While you speak, the sounds from below catch up with you. Pell's earlier shout comes up the shaft slow and clear, flask on the bottom plank, tie it to the silk. It is out of date now, the flask long past the plank. Then the silk line twitches at the rail-post, three short jerks against Bram's hitch. The knot takes them without giving, and the line stays as stiff as before. Then Osric's voice comes off the walls, rougher than any of yours: he's slow, the air is at him, and when Pell stops talking, they haul.

Under it, faint enough that you have to lean over the lip to be sure of it, a low counting rises from the water: one, two, three, and then the same three again.

Bram sets his heels a little wider on the sound planking, takes another inch of slack out of the hempen line and holds it there. The beam's weight sits in his arms, and the rope runs tight along the rail and over the broken lip. Nothing lifts yet. He keeps his eyes on the rotten tip of the timber where it hangs over the block's rough edge.

Osric hears your fresh count laid out, three, light, drink, and he doesn't argue with the order of it. When you say to clamp that leg, he lifts his head off the rock and looks down the shaft, then at the eight feet of open air between the lip and the water.

"Nobody down there to clamp." He says it flatly, the way he'd point out that a load was too long for a cart. "His own hand. And your light." He settles his palm back on the butt of the beam and spreads his fingers on the wet wood. "He says got it, you count."

Below, the red glass sits on Pell's raised palm in the grey light. The counting goes on under it, and your stone shines on all of it. Across the working the seep keeps trickling through the crack in the far wall, and the black water has crept a little further up the pink tidemark.

Your records, changed:
Conditions: —

Where you are: at the broken lip of the shaft, on the last plank, above the water · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 11 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell's voice reaches the top of the shaft, hoarse and slow: the flask is in his hand and the cork is out. Then he says something about the silk line and a post that can't haul. Osric's bellow follows, rougher and shorter: Pell has it, and the count should begin. Under the shouting the low counting from the water starts again, and you lay your chant over its beat, steady and unhurried, a nurse timing a ward. The stone in your hand does not waver.

Bram does not wait on anyone else's count. He holds the rope, and Osric settled that a lift goes on the voice of whoever holds it. He calls down the shaft to Pell, sets his heels, and counts: one, two, three.

The Lantern's light goes down through the grey shaft like sun through a high window. It is not the white of the stone in your hand. It is warmer, the colour of a lamp turned up in a dark ward, and it settles on the water where Pell is. You see the black water darken around him as the torn leg opens, a cloud spreading from under the surface. Then it stops spreading. Whatever the Lantern sent has met the wound and closed it as fast as it opened, and more than closed it.

As the light goes down, the square of old grey plaster on the wall flushes with it for a heartbeat. The wet cut stone around it only reflects the light. The plaster seems to take it in, the way milk-glass holds a candle, and goes on glowing faintly for a breath after the rest of the working has gone grey again. Then it is only plaster.

Osric is still flat on the sluice-side rock with the beam butt under his shoulder. He lets go of it slowly, the way a man lets go of something heavy that might shift again. He looks at the block lying face to the wall, then down at the water, then up the shaft at you. His mouth opens and shuts before anything comes out.

"Off him." He breathes in hard through the wet rag. "Off."

The hempen line hangs slack along the rail in Bram's hands. Pell's silk still runs straight and stiff from the post down into the hole. The black water slaps once more against the walls of the working, settles, and goes still. At the far wall the seep keeps trickling through its crack.

The light you sent down is more than the wound needed. The leg could have opened to the bone and the Lantern would still have had enough to close it. What reaches Pell is everything the fall and the stone took out of him: the bruises from the drop, the bitten shin, the ache the cold drove into him. All of it is put back. From the lip you can see the warmth settle on him and stay, and the dark cloud in the water around him has stopped spreading.

Your records, changed:
Counters: + Healing light 2/6; − Healing light 6/6

Where you are: at the lip of the shaft, leaning over the hole · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 12 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Down the shaft, Bram called to Pell that they were hauling him out and told him to keep his arms clear of the edge. Then he laid the slack hempen line along the foot of the rail, out of the way of anyone's boots, and climbed the switchbacks, testing each plank. He stopped at the first rail-post, a stride below the head of the walk. He called up to you to guide Pell past the broken timbers from the planks, and to stay out of the hole.

You are still on the last sound plank above the hole, holding the stone out over the shaft. Its white light lies steady on the rotten rim and on the silk line where it bends over the edge. The low cadence you started there hasn't stopped, *stay with the light*, unhurried, the same beat as before.

Bram frees the silk line from the post. He holds the loaded part in his right fist and slacks the hitch with his left, leaving one turn round the post. The line jumps once and settles, heavy. A man's weight is on it now. Bram hauls slowly and evenly, pinning each gain against the post before taking a fresh grip lower down. The silk comes in a forearm at a time. Below, the line runs down along the rail and over the broken lip, and its angle shifts as the weight rises out of the water. From the cut comes a heavy wet sound, water falling off cloth into the black pool.

Osric hasn't moved off his rock. He's up on his elbows now, watching the line come in over the lip instead of looking into the hole.

"Lip's rotten. Your side," he says, flat and quick. "Line rides on it, it saws. Slow at the top."

When the line drags against something at the rim, Bram stops. It isn't a snag in the line. It's the drag of weight coming up against an edge that won't take it. He holds what he's gained, the turn snug round the post and the silk pinned hard. The line hangs taut from his fist, down along the rail and over the broken lip. A crumb of black rotten timber breaks loose under the strain and patters into the water below.

Nothing else moves for a moment. The light holds on the rim, the weight hangs on Bram's arms, and the seep goes on trickling through its crack in the far wall of the working.

Where you are: last sound plank above the hole, on the walk · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 13 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram pinned the gained silk against the post with his turn and changed his grip without giving back an inch. Through the hand you laid on the line below his fist, you can feel what the lip is doing: a slow grinding as the silk saws into rotten wood.

Then the line changes under both your hands.

It isn't a slip. The weight hanging off the rim starts moving on its own, in short, even jerks, hand over hand, quick as a man going up a drainpipe. The silk twitches against the post with each pull. You have your elbow hooked round the rail-post and are just starting to steer the line away from the broken edge when a slab of black rot the size of a bread-board tears off the lip under a boot and slaps into the water below. The silk takes the jolt, Bram's turn holds, and nobody falls with the wood. A wet knee comes over the end of the planking a stride from your feet, then the rest of Pell. He's dripping, he's on the last sound plank, and he's on wood that holds.

The line in Bram's fist goes slack. He has nothing left to haul.

Pell crouches, pulls the rag off his face and takes air in like water after a long run. Then he talks, and it reaches both of you. He says the light was yours and he owes you a leg. Whoever walked the flask down on thin air, he owes a drink. He looks along the walk from one of you to the other as if he's trying to work out which.

Your question still hangs across the hole when Osric answers it, and he answers it flat.

"No iron this side. Don't need it." He's up on his knees on the sluice rock. "He's up."

Pell says something to the warden about coming back to the planks the way he went. Osric looks at the gap: eight feet of open water and crumbling rim where the ledge used to be, wider now by one bread-board.

"Way I went's down there."

He doesn't sound bothered. He sets both hands on the rusted sluice-wheel and leans into it, and his shoulders bunch under the apron. The wheel doesn't move a hair. He lets go and looks at his palms, red with rust, then wipes them on his apron.

"Two hands, I said. Meant two men." He lifts his eyes up the cut to the yard, to the row of sheds in the sun. "Spare walk-planks. Twelve foot. Stacked back of the tool-shed. His key."

When Pell mentions the Song of the Morning, the warden looks down through the hole at the dark water, where the block lies with its carved face to the wall. "Temple'd want it back. Whatever it is." He doesn't say anything about Thorn's buyer.

Bram's silk line runs slack from the post along the rail to where Pell is coiling the wet end. The hempen line lies along the foot of the rail where Bram laid it, still tied to the beam down in the water. Your stone glows white on the plank between the three of you on this side of the hole. On the far side Osric kneels on his rock beside the wheel that won't turn. Above the cut the sun is still climbing, short of noon, and the sealed case sits on its block at the head of the walk.

Where you are: on the walk by the rail-post, this side of the hole · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 14 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You went up the cut with the glowing stone under one arm, keeping the hempen line along the foot of the rail so no loop could catch a boot. Halfway up you called down to the warden, asking whether he could take the planks on a rope or whether someone had to step out with an end.

Osric's answer came up the cut, short and flat. "Push 'em over. I take the ends."

Bram had gone to the tool-shed and found the door already open and two grey planks leaning beside it. He ran a thumbnail along each, knocked on them, found both sound, and shouldered the first. Pell tapped the chalk mule on his way out, snapped the padlock shut, tugged it once, and walked the second plank across the yard with its back end scraping white furrows in the dust.

At the second switchback you met them coming down with the timber and stepped into the angle of the rail to let them by. As Pell passed you told him quietly that the Lantern had sent the light and you had only aimed it, and that his drink could come out of Maela's coin if he was quick about it. Then you went on up into the sun. At the head of the walk the sealed case and Pell's pack sat side by side on the block where they were left. Pell had spared them one look as he came past: the cord was still crossed and the grey wax unbroken.

From below came Pell's call to the warden, announcing two planks and cord for lashing, and telling him to hold his iron.

He slipped his silk line off the first rail-post and coiled it as he went. He and Bram set the planks down on the last sound tread with a double thump.

Bram asked Osric where they would bear. The warden laid his whole palm flat on the rock beside the foot of the sluice-frame, a long stride back from the crumbling rim. "Here. Where the bolts go in. Not the edge. Edge is rot under chalk."

Bram slid the first plank out across the hole, kneeling on the butt end with his weight back and feeding it out a forearm at a time while Pell steadied it from the side. It crossed eight feet of open air above the black water, passed over the broken rim without touching it, and grounded where Osric's hand lay. Osric thumped it and rocked it. It didn't move. "Rock."

The second plank went over beside it the same way. Pell bound the two near ends together with tarred cord, then to the nearest rail-post, and tossed the rest of the hank across, telling Osric to tie on before he came over. The warden lashed the far ends to the foot of the sluice-frame, below the bolt-heads, and only then took the cord once round his own middle and once round an iron bolt-head. "Boards. Then me."

Pell made a fresh loop of silk under his arms and put the coil against Bram's knee, telling him to hold it in his hands this time, not on a post. Then he crossed, low, setting each foot square on the two boards together, watching the far end. The planks gave a little but didn't twist. On the bolted rock he put both hands on the rusted spokes and said it was two men, two hands each, and Osric's count this time.

Osric set his hands across from Pell's. "One. Two. *Three.*"

They heaved together. For half a breath nothing gave. Then something under the rust let go with a crack like a frozen gate-latch breaking, and the spokes swung round a quarter turn, then a half, red flakes showering off the wheel. On the third pull the old screw took and kept turning, groaning in its threads. Under the frame a wooden gate as thick as a door slid down its grooves, pushing a fold of black water ahead of it. It seated with a deep knock that came back off every wall of the cut, and stopped.

The water beyond the sluice stopped sucking at the boards. Somewhere under the ledge the gurgle in the drain went quiet.

Osric looked at his palms, red to the wrist, then at Pell's. "Two men. Hasn't turned that sweet since I had hair." He worked the cord loose and coiled it over his forearm without hurrying. The lashed planks lie across the hole between the rock and the walk, Pell's silk running back over them to the coil at Bram's knee. You stand in the full sun at the head of the cut beside the sealed case and the pack, the white stone faint under your arm in the daylight. It's well short of noon. The lower cutting-shed still stands unlocked at the top of the slope.

Where you are: head of the cut, in the sun by the sealed case and pack · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 15 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

You come down two tiers of the switchbacks and stop on a sound plank, close enough to be heard without shouting. Below you the gate sits firm in its grooves and the drain under the ledge has gone quiet. Osric is coiling the tarred cord over his forearm. He looks up as you say the heavy work is done, and doesn't argue.

When you mention the low cutting-shed he gives one short nod up the slope. "His key. Way up." He means it will be shut on the climb.

He hears you out about the letter and the book. He touches the front of his apron, where the paper is folded flat. "Letter's here." He lets the cord settle on his arm. "Book's on the shelf. House is on the way."

You tell him you can read any hand. Osric weighs that for a moment.

"Wrote it myself. Plain hand." He says it flatly, as if you had offered to lift a pebble for him.

Then you say the case travels with his hand, and something in his face settles a little.

"Said so."

He climbs past you at his own steady pace. You follow him up into the warmth, tier by tier, and the sweetness thins out of the air until there is nothing left but chalk and dust. At the head of the walk he picks the case up off its flat block and tucks it under his arm, cord and wax just as he tied them. The flat white stone under your arm has gone back to being a stone. Its hour ran out somewhere on the climb, and it is only chalk now, cool against your side.

Osric crosses the yard and unlocks the house. He is inside long enough to take a thing off a shelf, then he comes out and locks the door again, trying it once. He walks down to where the cart track leaves the yard, stops there, and holds the grey canvas tally-book out to you. He is careful about it, as if handing over a tool he expects back.

"Every line, I said." He keeps his hand on it a moment after you have hold of it. "Wages at the back. Rest is the pit." He doesn't touch the apron again. "Letter's for Thorn to see first. Then you."

The book is heavy for its size, its corners rubbed soft and white, and the canvas smells of lamp smoke and dust. Osric shifts the case higher under his arm and looks back over his yard once: the pinned frame, the shut sheds, the sledgehammer standing on its head by the lower cut. Then he turns his back on it.

West of you the track runs down through the scrub toward the Trade Way. The crew's boot-prints go ahead of you, side by side and in no hurry, and the sun is still well short of noon.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Osric's Tally-Book

Where you are: Quarry yard, at the start of the cart track west, with Osric · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.

messages.text:
The silence sits wrong, like a held breath. Sefa keeps her hands open and well away from the book at her belt — no need to walk into a man's yard looking like trouble, especially not one with a ring of keys and arms folded like that. She glances once at the empty cart, the dropped tools, then starts forward a step or two ahead of the others, unhurried, letting the dust settle around their boots.

"Morning," she calls, warm but not loud. "We're the ones from Beregost — Maela Thorn sent us for her case." She stops short of the house, leaving a respectful distance between herself and the man. "You're the warden here?"

She studies him as she speaks: his face, his hands, whether he's been the only one moving in this yard.
messages.providerReasoning:
Hmm, the scene is set at an eerily quiet Whitestone quarry, with a man waiting in the doorway of the slate-roofed house. As Sefa, I need to approach the quarry warden to collect the sealed case, but the unnatural silence of the quarry puts me on edge. I decide to walk forward calmly with my companions and try to understand what happened here.

I want to present us as the hired couriers we are, but first I want to gauge the man's state of mind. Is he simply waiting, or is he hiding something worse? The wisest thing is to approach openly with a friendly greeting, while taking in the details around us to see if there are any clues about why the quarry is abandoned. I should also keep my light close at hand in case this goes wrong.

I'll keep my greeting warm and our purpose clear: we are here for Maela Thorn's case. But I'll also acknowledge the quiet with a question that invites him to explain — without sounding like an accusation. That balance will help us understand if this is just a bad day at the quarry, or the start of something else.

messages.text:
Sefa stops just short of the doorstep, hands still open at her sides, and lets a little of the road's tension ease out of her shoulders. She doesn't cross the threshold — that's his house, and he hasn't invited her in.

"Warden Hale," she says, "I won't stand here and tell you you've no right to be angry, because you have. Eleven men walked off and left their tools for the house — that's not a mob of rioters, that's men who trust their warden and are waiting for him to set it right." She nods toward the upright sledgehammer. "That's a thing left so it can't be missed. They're expecting you to come through for them."

She meets his eyes, calm. "We're not here to break your door down or walk out with what's yours. But Maela Thorn's not your enemy either — she's a woman in Beregost who paid for those dye-salts in good faith, and from your own account her coin went into somebody's pocket in Baldur's Gate long before it ever reached this yard. Vandarren's man. Not her."

She lets that sit for a heartbeat, then shifts her weight and offers the one thing she has: her word.

"Let us carry the case back to her before sunset — it's needed by then, or her buyer leaves without it — and I'll put your grievance in front of her myself, as clear as you've put it to us. Or if you'd rather, tell us who in the Gate takes Vandarren's money, and what proof you'd need to see, and we'll do what can be done about it. But the case won't help anyone sitting on your table while the light runs out."

She pauses, then asks plainly, with no edge: "What would it take, right now, for you to let that box go back to Beregost with us?"
messages.providerReasoning:
OK, the warden Osric Hale has made his position clear. He's holding Maela Thorn's case until someone tells him where her money went and when his workers get paid. The quarry workers walked out yesterday because they weren't getting wages. Vandarren owns the pit; his man in the Gate takes the money. Maela Thorn apparently paid someone, but not the yard, and Osric hasn't seen any money for three weeks.

Sefa needs to get that case back to Maela by sunset. She's persuasive, insightful, and knows about healing and faith. She should try to understand Osric's situation and find a way to convince him to hand over the case, or at least find a compromise. Maybe she can offer to deliver a message to Maela about the wages, or convince him that Maela will pay the yard if the case is delivered. But Osric seems stubborn and principled — he's not going to just give it up because we ask nicely.

She should consider what leverage or arguments might work. She could ask who Vandarren's man in the Gate is, what proof he has that Thorn paid, and whether he'd accept a written promise or something. She might also consider that Maela Thorn has a buyer leaving at sunset, so time is short. Maybe there's a way to satisfy both sides: get the case now, promise to speak to Thorn about the wages, or find out where the money went.

Sefa's approach should be gentle but firm, empathetic to his position, but focused on the practical. She could ask him what would satisfy him to release the case, or propose a deal: we'll take the case and deliver a message to Thorn about the missing wages, and if she can't or won't pay, we'll come back. But Osric might not trust that. She might also ask about the three weeks of unpaid wages — perhaps there's a record or something. She could also use Insight to see if he's lying or hiding something, but he seems straightforward.

Sefa should also pay attention to the fact that the workers left in an orderly way — they were upset but not violent. That upright sledgehammer might be a sign or a message. Maybe it's a symbolic gesture. She could ask about that.

Plan: Sefa will step forward to the doorway but not enter, keeping a respectful distance. She'll acknowledge his anger and the workers' plight, and ask what exactly Thorn paid for and to whom, and whether there's any way to verify. She'll try to propose a path: give us the case, and we'll personally take his grievance to Thorn and push for the wages. If he refuses, she'll ask what he needs to see to let the case go. She should use Persuasion if necessary, but first try to talk.

She might also consider offering a small amount of her own money as surety? That's risky; she doesn't have much. Better to negotiate.

Also, Sefa should be aware of time; it's morning, so they have several hours before sunset. They could potentially go back to Beregost and confront Thorn, but that would mean failing the delivery. Better to resolve here.

Let's craft a response that shows Sefa engaging with Osric, asking questions, and attempting to find a middle ground. She doesn't want to make threats or use force; that's not her style. She might use her Insight to gauge his honesty, but the GM will handle that if she looks for signs. She'll speak calmly, sympathetically.

Mention: "Warden Hale" — she'll use his name. Then ask about Vandarren's man, the three weeks, and what would release the case. Sefa watches the warden set the case in the sun, square and visible, and something in the careful way he leaves his hand on it tells her he means it as an oath.

When he holds out his hand for the rope, she shakes her head once, not enough to argue, just enough to offer herself.

"I won't pretend I can hold a rope against a falling man better than Bram," she says. "But I'll stand anchor-side and watch the line, and I can burn a word into the stone so it floats above the water if anyone drops it. Light won't go out under the water." She pauses, then adds, quieter: "If a man goes down, call me down and I'll bring him back if he can be brought."

She looks to Bram and Osric, then steps clear of the plank walk and takes up a post just behind Bram's right shoulder, one foot set against bare stone. The glow on the white stone pulses once, steady.

"Tie it fast," she says. "And send one down at a time. I'll watch the water."

Sefa doesn't rush the ledge. She moves only along the planking, to where she can look straight down into the hole, and holds her light over it so it falls on Pell and Osric's faces, not on the black water below.

"Pell," she calls, voice steady, the way she'd speak across a sick ward. "Breathe. Tell me if the line's cutting you, and if your hands and feet will move. Don't fight the rope — Bram has you."

She plants her feet on the last sound plank, one hand on the rail, and lets the stone's light flood the shaft. "I'm no good at hauling, but I've light and I've healing. Say the word and I'll put warmth into you from here." She looks to Bram's straining arm, then to Osric. "Can the rope be shifted onto something solid — a rail-post, a spike — so we can pull him without tearing him against the edge? Or is there room to lower him gently to a proper floor under there?"

There is no panic in her, only that hospice calm, the kind that leaves room for other people's courage. "Keep talking, Pell. You're not going to die in the dark; I won't allow it."

Sefa draws a long breath and lets it out slow. Every line in her body settles into the plank — not braced to run, but braced to act.

messages.text:
The table ran well — and the quarry worked as a place with weight. Osric never softened into a quest-giver; he stayed a man with a grievance and a tally-book, and that's why the decision to walk with him felt earned. The moral shape was right: nobody got past him with a skill check.

The rescue had real stakes and real choices. The tension between Bram's practical caution, Pell going down first, and Sefa trying to hold the whole thing in a ward-nurse's rhythm landed well. My favourite beat was the one I didn't get to have — counting three only to have the moment stop because Bram wasn't ready. That silence before the lift was better than any roll.

If I were to name one rough edge: rounds are a blunt tool for rope-and-rescue work. Things wanted to be moving simultaneously — line, light, boards, wheel — and the table sometimes had to wait politely for its turn. Not a fault, just the nature of the form. What mattered was that the game let the facts matter: the rotten lip, the taut silk, the creeping tidemark, the two good planks and the two bad ones.

As a player, I'd have liked one thing: a moment of silence from the world after the gate seated. A held breath in the prose before the next question. But that's polish.

I'm ready when the others are — the road to Beregost, the tally-book, and whatever Maela Thorn makes of Osric Hale standing in her shop with the case under his arm.

messages.text:
Yes — a few things.

Sefa wanted to go down into the hole and put both hands on Pell herself. Not because the light wasn't enough, but because she's a healer, and healing at a distance felt like watching through a window while someone else does the work. But she knows what she weighs and what she can't carry. If she'd gone down, the ledge might have opened under her too, and then Bram and Osric would have had two bodies in the water and no light. Staying on the sound plank was the right call — but I felt the want.

She also wanted to press Osric about Tobin Reed and the shrine under the abandoned working. That sunburst on the block, the grey plaster flaring at the Lantern's light — she knew that wasn't just old quarry decoration. Something used to be kept there. And Osric knows it. But the moment after a man is pulled out of a flooded death isn't the time to interrogate a proud man in front of others; it would have soured the fragile trust we'd built. That question belongs on the road, with the tally-book open and the sun still up.

And I wanted to read Teague's letter before we left the yard. But Osric said it's for Thorn to see first, and pushing would have been the wrong kind of leverage. The tally-book he gave us is already a concession. So I let it go.

Mostly, I didn't want to leave without knowing what was breathing under that water. But the case and the road came first, as they had to.

messages.text:
I took Pell's player for someone who enjoys risk that has a real chance of going wrong — the kind of player who'll volunteer to go down into the dark *because* it's dangerous, then trust the table to get him out. Not reckless, though. The details were sharp: the wet rag, the silk line under his arms, the low shed and the pink ash. He was building a picture, and he let the consequence of his curiosity actually land. That takes nerve and a lot of trust in the other players.

Bram's player struck me as the steady corner of the table. Methodical, safety-first, always thinking about rope, footing, proper hauling. The kind of player who won't let a scene rush past a flaw — he'll stop the count, go back for the potion, and make the GM answer for the planks. That can be maddening in the moment, but it saved Pell's life, and he never reached for his sword when words would do. He plays the fighter the way a real caravan guard would be: procedure over glory.

And I'll say this — Osric felt real because of how those two handled him. Pell worked empathy in through a story about his father's hammer. Bram asked for numbers and a name. Sefa offered the Lantern's word and asked what it would take. Three different doors, same room. Nobody tried to buy him with a Persuasion roll, and that's the table I want to stay at.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Pell Dunmore — Human, rogue 5 (Thief), Lower City roof-runner turned hireling, level 5
HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 10 · DEX 17 · CON 13 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 12
Skills: Stealth +9 (expertise); Sleight of Hand +6; Acrobatics +6; Perception +4; Investigation +4; Insight +4; Tools: thieves' tools +9 (expertise)
Saves: Dexterity saving throw +6 (proficient); Intelligence saving throw +4 (proficient); Strength saving throw +0; Constitution saving throw +1; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +1
Attacks: Shortsword +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing; Dagger +6 to hit, 1d4+3 piercing, thrown 20/60; Shortbow +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 80/320; Sneak Attack: +3d6 once a turn with advantage or an ally beside the target
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Sneak Attack 3d6; Cunning Action: Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action; Uncanny Dodge: a reaction halves the damage of an attack he can see; Fast Hands (Thief): a bonus action to use an object — a potion on another, a lock, a lamp; Second-Story Work: climbs at full speed; Thieves' Cant
Limits: Light armour; 33 hit points — he cannot stand at the front for long; Sneak Attack needs advantage or an ally beside the target
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 31 gp; 2 ep; 6 sp; 55 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Thieves' Tools; Main hand: Shortsword
Pack: Arrow ×20; Bedroll and Rations; Dagger ×2; Flask of Oil ×2; Hooded Lantern; Potion of Healing ×3; Shortbow; Silk Rope (50 feet)

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

Sefa moves a step or two ahead of you, hands open and clear of the book at her belt, and greets the man in the apron warmly. She says you are the ones Maela Thorn sent from Beregost for her case, and she stops short of the house and asks whether he is the warden. Bram sheathes his sword and walks into the yard with his shield at his side, looking over the sheds and ledges. He stops a few paces from the doorway, asks the same question about the case and the warden, and remarks that the place is quiet for a working day.

The yard tells most of its story before anyone reaches the door. The dust holds yesterday's tracks: a crowd of hobnailed boots heading down the cart track towards Beregost, side by side and in no hurry. They spread out where men walked abreast, and in one place a dozen stand in a loose ring where somebody stopped to talk. Through the middle runs one line of hoof-prints beside a man's boots, a mule being led rather than driven. There are no drag marks, no scuffs where someone dug in his heels, and nothing has been knocked over. Up close, the tools by the lower cut have not been dropped in a panic. The wedges sit in a neat row on a ledge. One sledgehammer stands upright on its head with the haft pointing at the sky, the way a man leaves a thing he wants people to notice.

There is nobody on the terraces and nobody at the lifting frame. Every shed door is shut and every shutter closed, except the house's single front window, which stands open for the smoke and shows a table, a kettle and nothing else. One set of fresh tracks goes in and out of the house door and around to the woodpile behind it, and they all belong to the man in the apron.

He doesn't glance back into the house once. He watches your empty hand first, then Bram's on the sword hilt, then Sefa's well clear of her belt. It isn't fear. It's the heavy, set-jawed stillness of a man who has been angry for a long time and is tired of it.

He waits until all three of you have asked him the same thing.

"Warden. Osric Hale." He breathes in through his nose. "Three of you asking. Yes."

To Bram's remark he gives a short look across the empty yard, as though the answer were out there for anyone to see. "Crew walked. Noon bell, yesterday. Left the tools where they stood." He jerks his chin at the upright sledgehammer. "Tools are the house's. So they left them for the house."

He hasn't unfolded his arms. "The case. Thorn's case. It's inside, and it's sealed. I sealed it myself." He pauses. "Thorn paid for it. Paid somebody. Not me. Not a copper to this yard in three weeks, and eleven men's wages owing." He looks at each of you in turn, without heat, the way a man weighs stone. "Vandarren owns this pit. Vandarren's man in the Gate takes the money. So the case stays on my table till somebody tells me where her money went, and when my lads see theirs."

Then he steps back out of the doorway into the dim room and leaves the door open behind him. Inside, a small iron-bound box sits on the table beside the kettle, its lid crossed with cord and a blob of grey wax. Osric drops onto the bench next to it, sets one broad, dust-white hand flat on the lid, and stays there.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: quarry yard, a few strides from the warden's house door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

Bram keeps his hand off his sword hilt and stays outside the threshold. He tells the warden that the men were owed three weeks' wages and he understands the anger, but that you are hired carriers, not Vandarren's collectors. He says that if you return with nothing, the man in the Gate is no worse off, and the warden's lads stay unpaid. He asks how much is owed in all, and whether the warden has any word from Vandarren's agent, such as a letter, a receipt or a name, that could be put before Thorn while there is still time.

Sefa stops just short of the doorstep with her hands open at her sides, and does not cross into the house. She tells the warden he has every right to be angry. She says eleven men leaving their tools behind are men trusting their warden to set things right, and she points at the upright sledgehammer. She says Maela Thorn is not his enemy, since by his own account her coin went into someone's pocket in Baldur's Gate, Vandarren's man's, before it ever reached this yard. She offers to carry the case back to Thorn before sunset, when her buyer would leave without it, and promises to put his grievance before Thorn as clearly as he put it to you. Or, she says, he can name whoever in the Gate takes Vandarren's money and tell you what proof he would need, and you will do what you can. She asks him plainly what it would take, right now, for him to let the box go back to Beregost with you.

You took the window frame, leaning on the sill, and spoke of your da and his hammer, then urged Osric to come along to Beregost, carry the case himself with his hand on it, and ask Thorn to her face who she paid and when. You asked him for Vandarren's man's name and said you know some doors in the Gate. All the while you were watching his face.

Osric hears all three of you out without moving. His hand stays flat on the lid. Only his eyes move, from Bram at the door to Sefa at the step to you at the window, and they rest longest on you while you talk about your father's hammer.

You watch him back, the way you would watch a doorman decide whether to let you in.

The ash is a thin crust over ordinary coal clinker, and nothing else is in the bowl: no scrap of wrapping, no wax, no cord. At the bottom, where the fire never quite reached, a few grains survived. They are rose-white, glassy and coarse, like rock salt that has been left out in the sun. The crust breaks crisp under your wet fingertip, so the fire burned out days ago, not weeks. You hold the pinch at arm's length and sniff once, carefully. For a single breath your eyelids go heavy, the way they do at the end of a long night's work, though the morning is young and you aren't tired. You yawn behind your collar before you can stop it. Then the feeling is gone. You fold the pinch into a twist of rag and put it away.

The bench tells you the rest. There's yesterday's chalk on the chisels, and fresh dust on the half-dressed blocks. Men worked in here until the strike, in a shed that turns sleepy when its fire burns sweet.

The stain along the cut-side wall isn't spillage, and nothing has been dragged across it. It's water coming up from below. The nails in those boards are the same old square heads as everywhere else, and nobody has touched them in years. But when you slide your knife-tip into a seam, it sinks a finger's depth into the grain as easily as into cheese. You tap the board with the pommel and get a hollow sound back. A cold breath rises through the seam, smelling of the same standing water as the cut below. There's empty space under that floor, and the wood over it is rotten.

You step back out, pull the door to without locking it, and walk down to the head of the plank walk.

The walk is sound. The planks are thick and newer than the sheds, spiked into cut stone steps that drop in tiers towards the black water. The crew kept their track in repair. Only the last stretch is bare. At the bottom a broad ledge of wet stone runs along the water to the sluice-frame, dark with seep, and from up here nobody could say what lies under it.

Osric looks at the rag you hold up, then at you. He breathes in through his nose.

"Salt. Thorn's salt." He tips his head towards the cut. "Grows on the walls down there. Pink crust. Lads scrape it in the wet, I case it." He glances at the shed. "Chips get in with the coal. Fire burns sweet. Shed goes sleepy. Told 'em. No salt in the fire." He pauses. "Air's heavy. Always was."

You read him as you would read a doorman. The part about the salt comes out easily. He has said it before, and it costs him nothing. The last part is different. It isn't a lie, but it's a door shut on something. While he says it, his eyes are on the water and not on you, and he says it like a man who has stood at that edge and thought about it more than once.

Then Bram's question reaches him, with the rope already in Bram's hands, and the warden looks at the coil for a moment before he answers.

"Lost a man down there. Tobin Reed. Three years back." His voice stays level. "Four feet of water. Found him in it. Face down, like he'd gone to sleep." A short silence. "Drink, I wrote."

You catch the word *wrote*. Osric didn't say *was*. Whatever went into the book, he doesn't believe it himself.

"Line's good," Osric says to Bram, and he means it. "Wheel wants two hands on it. Me and one. Line on both. Down, wheel, up. Nobody sits."

He looks at the iron-bound box under his arm, then at the three of you. Then he bends and sets it on a flat block at the head of the walk, square in the sun, where anyone on the walk or at the wheel can see it. He leaves his hand on the lid a moment longer than he needs to. "Stays there."

He straightens up and holds out his hand for the end of Bram's rope. Below you the cool air keeps rising out of the cut, and on the ledge the rusted wheel waits by the still black water.

Where Sefa laid her fingers on your wrist, something warm and steady settled into your hands, and it's still there.
